PRESIDENT’S 

REPORT 

LE RAPPORT DE 
LA PRESIDENTE 


As I write this the CCA/ACC Board has just completed its 
first President’s Council meeting at Nottawasaga Inn in Ontario. 
At this meeting all provincial presidents and all CCA/ACC 
Committee Chairmen discussed the affairs of CCA/ACC for two 
days. Many exciting plans are underway and we hope that CCA/ 
ACC will have a positive impact on each and every camp in our 
association in the next year. 

As the summer season is finally here, and we turn to our major 
work of the year, I hope that the summer is successful and happy 
for you. 

Janet Adamson, 
President. 



IN THIS ISSUE 

FIFTY YEARS of Canadian Camping — a half century of 
growth and service. In this issue the Canadian Camping Magazine 
looks to the past for re-identification of our roots and re¬ 
assurance of our path. Articles include canoe trips in Algonquin 
Parks, counsellor preparation and staff training. There is an 
interview of Adele Ebbs concerning the work and legacy of 
Taylor Statten. The International Camping Congress is featured. 
News from across the nation, program ideas and plans for regular 
features start the ball rolling for another 50 years of great 
Canadian Camping. 

DANS CETTE LIVRAISON 

CINQUANTE ANS de de camping canadien — un demi- 
siecle de developpement et de service. Dans cette livraison 
le Canadian Camping Magazine se souvient du passe pour 
retrouver nos origines et pour ressurer notre chemin. Ilya 
des articles au sujet des voyages a canot a “Algonquin 
Park”, de la preparation des conseillers et de la formation 
du personnel. II y a une interview avec Adele Ebbs 
concernant le travail et le legs de Taylor Statten. Le 
congres du camping international est represente. Pour 
faire demarrer encore cinquante ans forts de Camping 
Canadien, il y a des nouvelles de tout le pays, des idees de 
programmation, et des plans pour les articles reguliers. 


Pendant que j’ecris ce rapport, le conseil de I’ACC vient 
de terminer la premiere reunion du conseil des presidents 
au “Nottawasaga Inn” en Ontario. A cette reunion tous les 
presidents provinciaux et tous les presidents des comites 
ACC ont discute pendant deux jours les affaires de I’ACC. 
Ilya beaucoup de projets et nous esperons que I’ACC aura 
un effet positif pendant I’annee prochaine sur chaque 
camp qui fait partie de notre association. 

Comme I’ete est enfin arrive, et nous tournous vers notre 
travail majeur de I’an, j’espere que I’ete sera heureux et 
couronne de succes pour vous. 

Janet Adamson 
Presidente

REPORT FROM IAN FOWLER D’aprds Ian Fowler 

ATLANTIC REGION VICE-PRESIDENT Vice president de la region de I’Atlantique 


by Ian Fowler — Atlantic Region Vice-President 

The three provincial camping associations comprising the 
Atlantic Region all have new faces at the helm following recent 
annual meetings. For specific news of activities in these three 
provinces, check the individual reports below. 

Although Prince Edward Island does not have a provincial 
camping association at this time, efforts are continuing to 
establish such an organization, or to have their camps affiliate 
with N.B.C.A. or C.A.N.S. Perhaps my next column will have 
more concrete information on this subject. 

Even though all the Atlantic Associations are enjoying positive 
experiences, the highlight of the year is yet to come as the 
Canadian Camping Association in conjunction with N.B.C.A. 
will be hosting a Regional Conference, October 3 - 5 in Moncton. 
To add to the spice of the Regional Conference, Michael 
Brandwein, from Chicago, has been secured as the weekend’s 
keynote speaker. Having already inspired many Canadian 
camping leaders, it is expected the same will hold true for his 
journey east. 

Certainly the camping movement is becoming stronger in 
Atlantic Canada through the continued efforts of each provincial 
association, allowing for each camper who attends summer camp 
to have an enjoyable experience.

NEWFOUNDLAND 

* From the east coast the news is good for a 

—v revitalized if somewhat far flung associ- 

1 X ation in Newfoundland and Labrador. In 

Newfoundland, Frank O’Connor from 
Memorial University, has assumed the 
President’s position and is supported by an able group of new and 
veteran directors. Throughout the winter months, the N.L.C.A. 
has been busy, holding a one day winter workshop, along with 
several informational evenings in conjunction with their monthly 
board meetings. Recently, upwards of seventy camping people 
participated in their Spring Conference. A trip to Washington 
D.C. is in the plans for some members of the Association next 
year. 

yv NOVA SCOTIA 

/jX\ After providing many years of leadership to 
the Camping Association of Nova Scotia, 
CJn n rVS George Matthews recently stepped down from 
the President’s chair, to assume the role of 
^ u ^ Past President. Throughout the past year 
C.A.N.S. has been busy taking a look at its internal structure and 
association objectives. This resulted in numerous executive 
meetings leading to the association’s annual meeting held on 
April 26 in Truro. 

An inspired group of thirty camping personalities was present 
to share their views on how important C.A.N.S. was to their 
camp. Kelly Byrne, the director at Camp Big Cove, operated by 
the Halifax Y.M.C.A., was elected president and is looking 
forward to future challenges. 

NEW BRUNSWICK 

HvvH There are some personnel changes on the 
W/ Board of Directors. With Glenn Bamed’s 

move to Victoria Gillian Young takes his place 
to strengthen an already strong and enthusi¬ 
astic executive. The New Brunswick information pamphlet is 
ready for distribution. It gets full marks as a class act serving 
french speaking and english speaking parents equally well in an 
easy and attractive format. The Resource Catalogue Directory is 
in its final stages of preparation. 

In New Brunswick, Dan Soucy has taken over the helm of 
N.B.C.A. and is continuing to move the association in a forward 
motion. During the winter months, the Association held a winter 
workshop with Bill March, leader of the Canadian Everest 
Expedition as guest instructor and a workshop on programming 
for camp committee members, at which Wayne Perkins from 
Alberta was the keynote speaker. The association recently held its 
first provincial camping day with positive response being received 
around the province.

^ The Quebec Camping Association reports 
and acknowledges the great support of many 
energetic and committed members. One major 
project now in members’ hands is the new 
/ r\ ^ parents guide and directory. 

This summer, within the context of the accreditation program, 
four consultants visit almost sixty camps. This program requires 
that accredited camps be visited every two years. The camps that 
have had major changes during the year (change of director, for 
example), are visited as well. 

The QCA remains available for service to camp directors and to 
the public for all questions relating to camps throughout the 
summer. 

This year the summer meeting of camp directors will take place 
at Camp Trois-Saumons at the beginning of August. At this time, 
the members will again celebrate the 25th anniversary of the 
Quebec Camping Association. The reorganization of the directors 
of the French and English speaking camping community took 
place primarily in January of 1961.

REPORT FROM JAN JAMES, WESTERN REGION 
VICE PRESIDENT OF C.C.A./A.C.C. 

by Jan James — Vice President of C.C.A. /A.C.C. 

All the camps in the West are looking forward to the summer! 
The economic situation is posing a challenge to Camp Directors 
as they attempt to recruit campers — creative camp recruiting is 
the key! 

In March — 

Alberta welcomed new A.C.A. President, Bob Sperling, while 
April saw Saskatchewan saying “hello” to new S.C.A. President, 
Penny Wingert. Best wishes go out to Bob and Penny as they 
begin their responsibilities. 

Several Spring camping conferences and Workshops have been 
successfully completed. Alberta is looking forward to 2 counsellor 
training events in June. 



Expo *86 is underway, and several British Columbia Church 
camps are being represented at the Faith Pavillion. Visitors to that 
Pavillion are receiving literature from those individual members. 

I am off for 10 days in June to visit on behalf of C.C.A./ 
A.C.C. Three days in Fort Smith and ten days in Yellowknife 
should prove to be exciting. July sees me home in Alberta doing 
camp visitations, and then it is off to Australia in August. 

Happy camping, everyone 1

and the Evergreen Section of the American

CAMP CRAFTS 

by Brenda McFarlane — Eastern Region Editor 


Why do we use Crafts at Camp? As a rainy day activity ... a 
time filler ... a relaxer ... to make something to take home .. . 
to accomplish a new skill. Whatever the reason, we should choose 
a craft with a purpose geared to a particular age level. With 
children we all know that creativity holds no bounds. We as 
leaders must be enthusiastic and sell our ideas to the children — 
work together, learn together and much satisfaction will be 
gained. 

You may find a child who dislikes doing things with his hands. 
Do not force a child against his wishes but strive to find the 
reason for his reluctance. Perhaps it is lack of confidence or a 
desire for perfection, which should never be our ultimate goal. 
Try a teamwork project that could help this child overcome a 
hurdle. Working in a group is far less threatening than having to 
produce something on your own. 

Puppetry can be a fun activity 
at camp — especially for the ages A 
of 7 - 10 where imaginations run (» V] ) 

wild. From the simplest of wSK JJ 
puppets like the paper plate K Jr 

puppet to the one made from a 
styrofoam cup, craft stick and 

cardboard head with yarn hair, to \ / 

the most elaborate string puppets, U| 

little children will delight in doing v (J 

their show for the other campers. 

This story apron with its many pockets, 
g \ FEtT could unfold a dramatic story should the 
ft/j ) need arise. Especially helpful when working 
J puM jO? with very young children. 

Camp crafts do not have to be elaborate 
m ^ IPSJ or expensive. It has been my experience that 

r—| ^2^' some the best loved crafts were made 

from pine cones and walnut shells, rocks 
^ 5s==: === ===s:: ^ and other outdoor natural items. 


@o 

D@ 


One of the most rewarding things about working with children 
is just to listen to them — when I hear the expressions “neato” or 
“decent man”, I know that my crafts have been a success! I have 
captured their imagination and they, my heart! 

PAPER WEIGHT — Steam used postage stamps off letters 
and allow them to dry. Then glue them to a rock to completely 
cover. Once the glue is dry, coat them with a spray shellac and 
you have an original paper weight for Dad’s office. 

WALNUT SHELL SAILBOATS — As simple as this picture 
would indicate and always fun to see how well they sail. 




PLASTICENE 


- PAPER SAIL 


I— TOOTHPICK 


1/2 WALNUT 


OWL — Round pretzel for head, eyes will fill the holes, half 
cherries for beak and feet, walnut body and a long pretzel makes 
the perch. Glue onto felt or burlap and what youngster doesn’t 
like an owl. 

EYE GLASS LENS —* Save lenses from old eyeglasses. Trace 
the shape of the lens on a greeting card or attractive gift wrap. 
Apply glue to back of lens and press onto cut paper with design 
showing through lens. Using household cement, fasten a pin to 
the back and wear it proudly. 

PINEAPPLE — half a walnut plus half a small pinecone 
painted green for the top!

6 






Committee Notes/Les Notes Des Comites 


Archives Committee 

The role of the one man Archives 
Committee is to preserve a record of 
camping for all future generations. This 
can be accomplished by having each 
provincial association send its minutes, 
notices, programs, etc. to the Archivist at 
the camping collection at Trent University 
in Peterborough, Ontario. 

National Conference and 
Workshop Committee 

The CCA Action Plan directs this 
committee to run a National Conference 
every two years as well as travelling work¬ 
shops of a national nature in the same 
frequency. 

Because of the time required to plan, 
promote and produce an effective and 
dynamic conference the National 
Conference has been scheduled for 1989. 
The character and style of this conference 
is still taking shape and we are recruiting 
members and a chairperson for this 
exciting project. If you are interested in 
investing in the 1989 National Conference 
then contact the CCA Office. 

In the meantime the 2nd International 
Camping Congress in Washington D.C. 
effectively replaces the 1987 conference 
plans. Dave Sands is co-ordinating the 
CCA contribution with ACA. Look for 
more details on the Congress in this issue. 

A second sub committee is addressing a 
“travelling workshop” for 1988. The 
concept of a travelling workshop allows 
the sub committee to set up a specific 
workshop design dealing with specific 
matters and repeat it as often as necessary 
across the country reducing participant 
travel costs and time commitment. 

A third project is in the works—one 
which is a very exciting and worthwhile 
opportunity. This workshop, held in con¬ 
junction with the New Brunswick 
Camping Association fall conference will 
be conducted in Moncton from October 1 
— October 5. The workshop takes double 
aim at the new Camp Director’s Cur¬ 
riculum and at a Management Board 
Training Session. Fitness Canada has 
agreed to grant the funds necessary to 
bring one delegate from each province at 
no cost. 

This opportunity to inject your 
association with energy and stimulus 
should not be missed. Anyone who is a 
current member of their provincial 
camping association and who is prepared 
to act on the information of the work¬ 
shop when they return home is en¬ 
couraged to attend. The selection criteria 


for delegates (subsidized and non- 
subsidized) and a description of the work¬ 
shop is being sent to each province. 

The conference of NBCA is a bonus for 
workshop participants, especially in the 
light of its featured presenter — Michael 
Brandwein. Michael is an internationally 
renowned leadership and educational 
training consultant. He presents, with a 
dynamic and convincing presence, 
essential components of effective camp 
leadership. When you blend a profes¬ 
sional speaker, a professional entertainer, 
a professional educator, a professional 
lawyer and a professional actor, you get a 
professional camp counsellor named 
Michael Brandwein. 

As you can see there will be enormous 
amounts of information, material and 
skills that will be shared with delegates in 
the fall. 

Count yourself in and count your 
association in on the process of workshop 
— conference — growth. 

There are great things coming up and 
they are designed for you. Step forward, 
get involved and brighten the future! 

French Language 
Committee 

In 1985, a project attracted our 
attention — the publication of a list of 
the French language camps outside of 
Quebec. The publication was possible 
thanks to the collaboration of The 
Council of French Life in America. 
Twenty-four camps are included in the 
first edition and we hope to add all French 
language camps within two years. Your 
contribution is required, then, to help us 
identify the camps not included in the list. 
It is possible to obtain a copy of the list (a 
limited number are available) from our 
Provincial Association or from the office 
of the National Secretary of the CCA. 

Having been president of this 
Commission for less than one year, I 
would like to have representatives from 
different parts of Canada as members of 
the Commission. We presently have a 
contact in New Brunswick. If there are 
directors of French Language camps from 
Ontario and from another province 
(Western or Central Canada) interested in 
being part of the Commission, I would 
like to know so that we could develop 
some linguistic policies. In addition, we 
could circulate and share skills. and 
knowledge in French for the benefit of all 
of our fellow francophones. 

Gerard Bachand 
President

Garard Bachand

Fitness Canada and CCA 

Fitness Canada is hosting a four day 
conference on Fitness from June 8th to 
June 11th. Two hundred delegates from 
various facets of the fitness community 
will attend the summit in order to assess 
the fitness needs of the country now and 
in the future and to establish the future 
policy direction of physical fitness 
programs. 

Diane Blair (from Camp Gay Venture) 
will represent the CCA in Ottawa during 
the summit. She will be trying to interpret 
the new definitions for fitness in terms of 
the CCA. With Canada’s increased 
emphasis on lifestyle and positive 
attitudes toward physical activity Diane 
can present the camping cause as a natural 
choice. 

The impact of policy decisions at this 
level can be profound and we hope that 
Diane will be able to report of positive 
new directions for the shared objectives of 
Fitness Canada and CCA. 




Between 
The Covers 



Every learning disabled child should 
have the opportunity to attend summer 
camp. As with all children, these young 
people have the same basic needs ... to 
have fun and to be loved. The list goes on, 
there is no mystery to it since many of us 
have worked with these types of indi¬ 
viduals without ever realizing it. 

Doreen Kronick has prepared three 
convenient booklet guides for parents and 
camp directors. They are informative and 
brief. One is for camp directors of 
specialized camps. A second is a camp 
director’s guide on integration and a third 
is for parents of learning disabled 
children. 

The two camp directors’ guides cover 
the considerations and responsibilities 
needed to screen learning disabled 
children for their camp and what is 
needed to work with them. For a special¬ 
ized camp, experienced staff and the ratio 
of them to campers is important. Precamp 
training, then, is geared specifically to¬ 
wards the learning disabled child. 

For the director of a “regular” camp 
the question of integrating learning dis¬ 
abled campers can be determined by 
evaluating your camp program and asking 
the right questions. Kronick’s guide 
defines learning disabilities and then 
answers the common questions. 

The parent’s guide help the parents 
decide whether or not their child should 
attend a specialized camp or a camp that 
integrates these children into their 
program. Once this is decided, choosing 
the right camp for any child follows a 
similar route. Eventually, many of the 
same questions apply ... Is my child 
ready for camp? ... For how long should 
my child attend? . . . and how will I pay 
for camp? 

Once the parent has decided on a few 
potential camps, a parent-director 
interview and child-director orientation 
session would help. Kronick gives guide¬ 
lines to both the parent and camp director 
on potential questions and expectations.

utiles pour les parents des enfants 
avec les probtemes d’apprentissage, 
pour les directurs de camps qui 
consid^rent I’integration de ces 
enfants et pour les directeurs des 
camps specializes.

“SOME THOUGHTS 
FOR THE DAY” 

What a misfortune it would be ... if we 
could only work happily with those who 
saw things as we do. 

— Jane Erskine Stuart 

Even if you’re on the right track, you’ll 
get run over if you just sit there. 

— Will Rogers 

To feel you have done what should be 
done raises you in your own eyes. 

— Eugene Delacroix 

Nobody is sicker than a counsellor who is 
sick on a day off. 

— Ray Bowers 

You gotta do unto others as you would 
have others do unto you. And with 
thoughts like that running through your 
head, there’s nothing good that you can’t 
do. 

from the song 
“Talk About Peace ” 
by Joe Lawrence Hampson 


“Where Have All The Flowers Gone?” 

Do you remember Peter, Paul and Mary? Who, over 35 — or is it 40, could forget 
them? The youngsters — those under 35, or is it 40 — certainly know the legacy — 
“Puff the Magic Dragon”, “Where Have All the Flowers Gone”, “Kisses Sweeter than 
Wine”. Many of these wonderful songs of the folk era are sung around our campfires. 

But wait! These people are old! Old people don’t sing folk songs! Peter and Paul are 
going bald, and is that gray I see in the hair which they still have? Glasses? Mary, her 
figure bordering on the matronly, has lost the bloom of youth. What has happened? 

Reeling with the shock of seeing these aging idols of my university days, I closed my 
eyes. Only the music — miraculously the years disappeared; it had the same magic, the 
same intensity, it wove the same magic spell as it did all those years ago when my world 
was young. 

“But,” I hear you cry, “What has this to do with camping. This magazine doesn’t 
carry T.V. program reviews.” 

It is good to cast our minds back now and then — back to those days known 
somewhat cynically as “the good old days,” — the days when life was simpler. Our 
predecessors didn’t have to worry about drugs, or complicated government forms, or 
medical examinations for foreign staff, or how to weave campers away from a life 
centered around television, computers and video games. They didn’t have to worry 
about coping with children from single parent families or deal with the inner hurt at 
seeing the change in an old camper whose parents had divorced over the winter, leaving 
her hanging in a world of divided loyalties. Yes, times have changed, the problems 
which campers have to cope with in their growing up has changed. The world has aged, 
and so have our campers in that the innocence of childhood is being denied them by the 
course of society. They are so much more aware. 

But wait! Close your eyes — travel back to your own “singing wilderness” — do you 
hear it! Laughter, songs, voices calling out in joy, white sails dancing on the lake, 
canoes softly slipping towards a cruising loon. The magic is still there. The magic of 
childhood has almost, but not quite, been stolen away from these children. It is we who 
can see the aging of the world who have the capacity not only to see, but to recreate the 
magic that we know is there, there within those children. We know this, but it is so easy 
to say, “the children come from a different world and we must adapt.” Adapt, yes, but 
how? It is too easy to fall into the trap of just “modernizing” our camps — more 
movies, more equipment, take out the tents, build the cabins, put in electricity, running 
water, more, more, more. 

We all recognize that children are still children, as they have been through the ages. 
Undoubtedly the culture shock which a child experiences in coming to camp is greater 
than it was in the past. Even our staff members find this, more than we did as young 
counsellors. Herein lies the challenge — we must work with our staff members to make 


8 











them aware of the depths of our philosophy and deal with the specific problems which 
arise because of this change of lifestyle. 

What is this I hear? A song about San Salvadore tucked between the old favorites? 
It’s new. It’s not Peter, Paul and Mary. Listen, there is a message; wait, they are getting 
a standing ovation for that one song, the audience is identifying with the message. The 
audience loves the old, but they appreciate the new because it has a valid message. It was 
sung in the tradition of Pete Seeger’s protest songs. The performance was enhanced by 
this and other new songs. The inclusion of new songs kept their performance alive — 
they weren’t just old fogies trotting out the tried and true for old time’s sake. Camps 
can’t just trot out all the old ideas for old time’s sake; we must recognize the need for 
new zest, but not by sacrificing the old — the things that our campers, and our parents, 
and we ourselves treasure. There must be a valid blend. 

The magic — we must hold on to the magic of the simple life — the life which 
epitomizes not only the escape from the city but the growth of awareness of the world 
around us and the people with whom we live. This simple life is good, it’s worthwhile. 
We must keep up with progress realizing the change in the background of our campers, 
BUT, we must remember the old magic and pass it on and not allow ourselves to be 
blown over by the wind of change. A tree bends in the wind, but held by its roots it 
sways gently and remains strong. 

Where Have All the Flowers Gone? Hopefully, they are in our “singing wilderness’’ 
to be enjoyed spiritually by our campers and to be taken home so that they might have 
flowers in December. 

Madelene Allen 
Camp Ouareau 

Les chanteurs de chansons folkloriques Peter, Paul et Mary ont recemment 
fait une tournee d la television. Bien qu’ils (et aussi I’auteur) aient vieiili depuis

applicable & nos vies. Le message que les camps donnent aux jeunes reste 
aussi pour la plupart Inchange. Les chanteurs de chansons folkloriques ont 
offert des pensees courantes dans leurs nouvelles chansons. Dans la meme 
fagon, les camps doivent fusionner leurs deux messages, en combinant les 
racines fortes avec les pointes et les branches qui poussent.

Cross Canada Water 
Relay Planned 

The purpose of the Cross-Canada 
Relay is to promote recreational canoeing 
while paddling in an event which draws 
attention to a regional or local issue that 
affects our waterways. 

The events are as diversified as our 
country and its people. Listed here are 
some of the happenings; as spring break¬ 
up approaches, more details will be 
available. 

EASTERN CANADA (Duncan Ford- 

Director) 

The water bottle will be dipped in the 
Atlantic during ceremonies which Federal 
Minister of the Environment, Tom 
McMillan, will be invited to attend. 
Rendezvous at connecting points will be 
established between the Maritime 
Provinces and Newfoundland. The 
paddlers will have the packet in Quebec by 
late June. 

CENTRAL CANADA (Daniel Gauvreau- 

Director) 

The packet (containing a water bottle 
with water from each area, a list of par¬ 
ticipating paddlers and an item indigenous 
to the region) will be passed from Quebec 
paddlers to Ontario paddlers in Ottawa. 

WESTERN CANADA (Betty Donaldson- 

Co-ordinator and Director) 

Each Western Province will organize a 
paddling event but direct contact between 
paddlers may not be possible at all border 
points. The Manitoba Recreational 
Canoeing Association is in contact with 
the Naturalists Association, Manitoba 
Camping Association, Manitoba Outdoor 
Educational Association, with plans to 
hold a summer-time event. Saskatchewan 
will organize a June trip on the Sturgeon 
River Weir that emphasizes the contrasts 
between that historic route as it was 
during fur trade days and today. A diary 
from the 1800’s will be updated. Alberta is 
planning a North to South trip that will 
include school children and that will draw 
attention to proposed river rerouting. 
British Columbia has two brigades 
planned: the Northern one honors 
Alexander MacKenzie, the Southern one 
goes from Hope to the (Vancouver) 
Harbour and is a part of Expo. Each 
British Columbia Zone is competing for 
the Dirty Water Award — the winner will 
publicize the dirtiest paddling water in 
their area. 

The Yukon claims to be “on top of it 
all*’ with the best water in Canada and 
would like to meet B.C. paddlers at the 
border. In the N.W.T., the Slave River 
Paddle is a race on the August long- 
weekend and marathoners are invited to 
try the White Water if they have sufficient 
skills.

PERSONALITY PROFILE Le Profil De Personnalite 


Taylor Statten 

50 years ago, Taylor Statten of the 
Taylor Statten Camps — Ahmek and 
Wapomeo — was the Founder and first 
President of the Canadian Camping 
Association. Three years previously, he 
had Founded and was the first President 
of the Ontario Camping Association. He 
is the only Canadian to have been 
President of the American Camping 
Association. CANADIAN CAMPING 
MAGAZINE conducted this Personality 
Profile with Taylor Statten’s daughter, 
Adele Ebbs, a Past President of the 
Ontario Camping Association, Archives 
Chairman for the C.C. A. and O.C. A. and 
a long-time director of Camp Wapomeo. 


AE: No, Camp Couchiching was before Geneva Park. Geneva 
Park didn’t exist in the Y’s eyes until 1908. It was taken 
over by one of the Y men, or it was given to one of the Y 
men and he started to develop it into a training centre for 
young leaders. But at the same time, Camp Couchiching, 
which was across the lake at Orillia, continued to be a boys’ 
summer camp until 1912. I think that was the last summer. 

CC: Then it changed its site and its name too, 1 guess. 

AE: That Camp Couchiching just stopped and as far as I know 
it went up to Torrance and became Pine Crest. 

CC: Who were the people that influenced your father at that 
time, that helped him with his direction-setting? 

AE: I know that Dr. Crocker, who was a Physical Education 
man, was a very important influence on him. C.M. Cope¬ 
land was another man who was important to him and sort 
of guided him on the straight and narrow. 

CC: Did Ernest Thompson Seton come in at this time or was 
that later? 

AE: Ernest Thompson Seton? No, he was later. I don’t think 
he had anything to do with Dad until they were doing the 
CSET bit. I don’t think there was any Indian influence at 
Couchiching. There was no Council Ring at Camp 
Couchiching as far as I know or have any record of or any 
pictures. 

CC: Maybe we could return to Ernest Thompson Seton when we 
begin to talk about the Taylor Statten Camps. 

AE: Yes. 

CC: There’s a really interesting story about P. T. Barnum. 

AE: Well, Dad always thought that he was related to P.T. 
Barnum. The “T” in Barnum’s name stood for Taylor and 
he did come from the same area. I think Pennsylvania. 
Dad used to spend hours, when he had hours, in New York 
City in the reference library trying to look up his ancestry. 
I think he must have found some connection to P.T. 
Barnum at that time. And we always thought that was why 
he was a showman and always enjoyed the circus. He loved 
circuses. We had a circus at Camp every year. No matter 
what the theme was, it was called a circus. 


INTERVIEW WITH ADELE EBBS 

CANADIAN CAMPING: 

Adele, it seems so logical that, in the first profile we are 
doing for the Canadian Camping Magazine in our 50th 
year, we have selected your father, Taylor Statten, as our 
Personality Profile because he was the founder and the first 
President of the Canadian Camping Association. What 
were early happenings that led your father into a career in 
camping? 

ADELE EBBS: 

Well, it was because he was in boys* work, head of the 
boys’ club of the Central YMCA and, therefore, became 
Director of Camp Couchiching which was up near Orillia. 
He was full-time boys’ work man, in charge of the Camp, 
and they had a large Camp in those days and some very 
eminent people went. 

CC: Prior to that, his early education ... he was born ... 

AE: He was born in Erindale in 1882, just out toward Cooks- 
ville, west of Toronto, practically part of Toronto now. It 
was called Springfield originally and that’s where his 
grandparents, both sets of grandparents, lived. They came 
up from Pennsylvania. Dad attended Streetsville High 
School but didn’t ever graduate from high school ... I 
don’t think. As a result of that, all his life he was craving 
more knowledge. He used to go back to the University and 
take courses from time to time. He was always interested in 
learning and interested in reading. 

CC: So, after High School, he began working for the YMCA 
which takes us to Camp Couchiching. 

AE: Yes, I think so, because he worked in the Post Office when 
he first came into Toronto and then quickly got into the 
YMCA. 

CC: You talked about Camp Couchiching — the first Camp 
he directed. 

AE: Yes. 

CC: With the Toronto Central YMCA. Was Couchiching what 
is now Geneva Park? 


Taylor Statten 


Ilya cinquante ans, Taylor Statten 
des camps Taylor Statten — Ahmek 
et Wapomeo — etait le fondateur et le 
premier president de I’association 
des camps du Canada. Trois ans 
auparavant, il avait fonde I’associ- 
ation des camps de I’Ontario et il en 
etait le premier president. II est le 
seul Canadien d’avoir 6te le president 
de I’association des camps de 
I’Amerique. Canadian Camping 
Magazine a dirige le profil de 
personnalite avec la fille de Taylor 
Statten, Adele Ebbs, une ancienne 
presidente de I’association des 
camps de I’Ontario, presidente des 
archives pour I’A.C.C. et pour I’A.C.O. 
et directrice de Camp Wapomeo 
depuis longtemps. 


10 









CC: P.T. Barnum drew people to him, particularly young 
people, and your Dad certainly did that, too. 

AE: He might have had the odd gene there, somewhere. 

CC: His “showman” gene. His “charismatic” gene. Would 
you think that was the strongest part of his personality, as 
a leader in camping, his charisma ... his ability to draw 
people to him? 

AE: Well he did draw people to him, but I always thought he did 
it in a very quiet way. Mind you, he did have great flashes 
of ideas and was very creative in presenting new ideas to 
his staff, but he was always sort of in the background him¬ 
self. He didn’t mind dressing up. He would dress up any 
way he was told to dress up, for circus day for instance, and 
he thoroughly enjoyed it. I didn’t know him in the days 
when he was an Evangelist, which he was, I think, during 
the war years or after the war years before the 20’s. I’ve 
met men who met him at Father and Son Banquets and I 
have one reference in notes by him of, I think it was in St. 
Catharines, where he had them (audience, congregation) 
really eating out of his hand. They stood up and came to 
the front to confess and all that sort of thing. In my 
memory, this was most unlike him, but apparently he used 
to do it. 

CC: Did he ever employ any of those techniques with campers 
at Camp? 

AE: Not really, no. 

CC: Or with his staff at Camp? 

AE: No, I don’t think he did. This is why it is so foreign to me 
to think of him as having sort of an aura of influence that 
was unique. Well, it was unique. 

CC: It certainly was and dynamic, too! So, from 1912 until 
1921, he had moved from being the Boys’ Work Secretary 
of the Toronto YMCA and had done some work in Ontario 
and Quebec for the YMCA and Boys’ Work, but then he 
became the National Boys’ Work Secretary of the YMCA. 
I guess camping wasn’t a part of his life then, was it? 

AE: No. He used to travel from coast to coast, once a year, 
talking to groups of YMCA and Father and Son Banquets 
and so on, and it was a very hard life really, in those days, 
especially when transportation was so difficult. I remember 
vividly him telling me about getting from New Brunswick 
across to Prince Edward Island on one of these boats where 
you were strapped in. When you were in open water, you 
would jump in the boat and paddle and, then, when you 
came to ice, you would jump out and run it along the ice. 
I found a picture, not of him, of that way of transpor¬ 
tation. He travelled back and forth during the War years. 
But he didn’t do any camping. Our family used to go to 
Geneva Park for the summer and he was involved in 
leadership training there. Eventually when we discovered 
the charm of Algonquin Park in 1912 or ’13, we used to go 
there for holidays in the month of September with no 
camping at all. I mean no “paying guests” . . . just 
friends. Always a lot of them, I might say. 

CC: It was during this period of time then, 1912 - 1921, that 
SOS came into the picture.... 

AE: Yes, during the war. 

CC: SOS means...? 

AE: Soldiers of the Soil. 

CC: What was his involvement with “Soldiers of the Soil”? 

AE: He just organized, or helped communities organize, young 
people to go out and work on the farms, in the Spring 
and Summer, then in the Fall for picking produce. 


CC: The SOS people who replaced those who would have been 
there if they hadn’t been at War? 

AE: Yes. They were teenagers who were too young to go to 
War. 

CC: Now, was this an idea of the YMCA or... 

AE: Yes, I am sure it was. 

CC: Was it because his work was so strenuous that he decided 
it was time to establish the Taylor Statten Camps, or was he 
just ready in his life to do that? 

AE: No, the Taylor Statten Camps just grew out of the fact that 
he found this campsite in Algonquin Park on Canoe Lake 
and, with his international relationships with the training 
group, they decided to have a national leaders’ training. He 
suggested that it be at Canoe Lake, so that’s what 
happened. And it rained for two weeks, I believe, that 
first year. That was 1920. By that time, the Boys’ Work 
Council was YMCA and Religious Education Council 
combined and they were the leaders who attended. The 
group that went up in 1920 included Dr. Myers for one, 
a minister I know, and two or three other ministers. 
Moyle was one of them; Charles Plewman and YMCA 
Camp Directors like Ace Milks. That first year, the two 
weeks was just training camp but it was so successful. Some 
of the men had brought their sons up and that made Dad 
think, “Gee, this is a good place for young men to be as 
well as leaders.” Therefore, in 1921, he had 60 boys as 
paying guests, campers, and that was when Camp Ahmek 
started, along with the second National Leadership 
Training Camp. 

CC: Was your Dad still involved with the YMCA in 1921 ? 


CC: And did that go on for a number of years? 

AE: No, it didn’t go on for much longer after that. I’m not 
sure when it stopped. But in 1927, you see, he became 
involved full-time, pretty well, with Pickering College, 
so sometime in the 20’s he must have left the Y. 

CC: And what was the Pickering College involvement, in 1927? 

AE: Well that’s when Pickering College opened up at 
Newmarket. Joe McCulley was made headmaster and Joe 
asked the Chief if he would be on the staff as Director of 
Character Education, I think it was called. From 1927 until 
the War started in ‘39 and then, of course, he had Ahmek 
in the summertime. 

CC: Now Ahmek was started officially with 60 boys and the 
leaders in 1921, then the girls’ Camp Wapomeo...? 

AE: Started in 1924. 

CC: Was your Mom the first Director of Wapomeo ... or 
your Dad? How did that happen? 

AE: Mother was officially the Director but she was never the 
same leader that Dad was at Ahmek. She always employed 
some person to be the front person, the active person, the 
Program Director I suppose we would call it. And Helen 
St. John, who was a teacher at Jarvis Collegiate at that 
time, was the first Program Director and then at the same 
time Margareta Spence was there the first summer but she 
became the Program Director after that and for a number 
of years at Little Wap. 

CC: Then Adele came along! 

AE: Yes, pretty much soon after that. Little Wapomeo con¬ 
tinued to operate on the one little island until 1929 (no, 
1928) and then we spread over onto the Senior Island. 
When the depression came, we closed down the little island 
and everyone moved over to the big island. That is when I 
started to be active. I was head of the Junior Section of the 
Camp and started in 1931. 


11 



CC: Your Dad had just an incredible ability to gather around 
him people who were dynamic leaders in themselves. It was 
one of his premier strengths, I think. Let’s talk about a few 
of these people. Maybe we could start with Ernest 
Thompson Seton and then discuss some of the other people 
your Dad attracted to Camp over those years. 

AE: Well, in the early days Ernest Thompson Seton was one 
but he was sort of a “fly-by-night” in a way. He only 
came up for a brief time, but he sure had his influence on 
the Camp and on everybody. And, of course, he started the 
Council Ring. One of the gentler and very important 
people was Jack Miner. Jack Miner and his wife used to 
come over to stay at Little Wap with the girls and Jack 
would go over to Ahmek and do the Nature work. Along 
with Jack Miner was Ernest Thompson Seton’s nephew, 
Stuart Thompson. He was a Torontonian and he and his 
wife were much different from the showman of Ernest 
Thompson Seton. Stuart Thompson was a very gentle man 
but he was there for years doing Nature. Alex Edmison, 

I suppose, would be considered one of the very important 
early leaders and ... 

CC: Excuse me, just before we leave Ernest Thompson Seton, 
your Dad was always the Chief in Council Ring. Ernest 
Thompson Seton wouldn’t step forward and fulfill that 
role? 

AE: I think he did. I don’t think he would let anyone be Chief 
except Ernest Thompson Seton. 

CC: Did he precede Ellsworth Jaeger or were they contem¬ 
poraries? It seems to me you can’t talk about the develop¬ 
ment of Council Ring without mentioning Jaeger as well as 
Seton. 

AE: I am not sure about that. I know that Ellsworth Jaeger had 
the Camp of the Red Gods, and I know that Ernest 
Thompson Seton went up there. That was as a guest or as 
a visiting VIP and, of course, Ellsworth Jaeger was only 
there for a couple of years. I don’t know what happened 
after that. 

CC: You referred to Alex Edmison .... 

AE: Alex was a very supportive person from the very beginning. 
He was a great collector of campers and staff. His associ¬ 
ation with Dad began in the Boys’ Parliament, which was 
one of the things that the YMCA ran. I don’t know when 
the Boys’ Parliament started, but it was in the late teens or 
early 20’s and Alex Edmison was Mayor of Toronto. So 
that was how Dad became involved with Alex. 

CC: Alex wasn’t the official Mayor of Toronto, but as a 
youth... 

ae; He was the Boys ’ Mayor of Toronto, and that was 
probably in 1921. 

CC: So was he ever on staff at Ahmek? 

AE: Oh yes, for years. I don’t think he was there the first year of 
Camp. Woody, Frank Wood, was sort of co-director with 
Dad the first year but that didn’t last long. Dick Van 
Valkenberg was another early person. Chick Hendry was 
there, I guess, that second year at Camp. 

CC: How about people who went on into Camping themselves, 
like Ron Perry, Blackie Blackstock. 

AE: Bernie Hodgetts.... 

CC: All of those people were on those early staffs, weren’t 
they? 

AE: Bernie Hodgetts wasn’t an early staff member. He was 
there during the War. The others were on staff though. 

CC: And then, of course, Hedley Dimock had a big .... 


AE: Hedley came to Camp, not until the mid 30’s, I think. I am 
just thinking because his book was published in ‘37 or ‘27? 
no ‘27 wasn’t it? 

CC: Which one — “Talks with Counsellors”? 

AE: Yes, when was it published? 

CC: I don’t know. Ed. Note: Published in 1939. 

AE: I am trying to think of Hedley Dimock and Chick Hendry. 
Oh, it would be in the late 20’s, sure. And who else was at 
that time? I must mention Chubby who was our Business 
Manager, Dad’s confidante. The whole Camp would have 
fallen apart if Chubby hadn’t been there to pull the reins 
and everything else. 

CC: He was there a lot of years.... 

AE: He was there . . . well I can’t remember whether he was 
there the first year of the training Camp because he had 
been in ill health and was up at Mowat Lodge and that’s 
how Dad got to know him. He was in the YMCA at 
Capreol. 

CC: That would be a railroad YMCA. 

AE: Yes, that’s where he was as a Y man and then he became 
ill and spent a winter at Mowat Lodge. Then, he came as 
Dad’s righthand man and he stayed with him forever. 

CC: George Chubb! Then, there is a whole group of people who 
went on to become really significant contributors to the 
medical profession, headed by your husband, J. Harry 
Ebbs. Did they go to Ahmek as campers, as medical 
directors, as both? 

AE: I would think they came as Camp doctors. I was interested 
to know that our family physician. Dr. Thomas, was 
physician to Camp Couchiching in 1905 so he was quite an 
old boy when we came along. We had doctors, and I don’t 
know who got the doctors to come in the beginning . . • 
they usually came with their families. My husband, Harry, 
was in medicine starting in 1926, so he was a medical 
student and had contact with doctors all the way through. 
He was responsible for getting the physicians to Camp. It is 
too bad he is not here to say when he started to do that. I 
know there were some doctors who were not his responsi¬ 
bility, sort of old family physicians who came the first year 
of Camp. Gradually, all the pediatricians started to come, 
of course, when Harry became involved . . . like Wilson 
McTavish who was physician to Upper Canada College 
(retiring at the end of this month) and Gar Hamblin and 
George McNaughton and King Rowan - Legg. 

CC: Peter Turner? 

AE: Peter Turner. Well, Peter actually had taken over for Harry 
and continued to get younger Pediatricians to come after 
Harry retired. So, we have had a good crop of Pedia¬ 
tricians. 

CC: Is your brother Taylor a Pediatrician? 

AE: He is a Child Psychiatrist and never has anything to do with 
medicine when he is at Camp, nor with psychiatry. He 
discourages any patients of his to go to Camp. He doesn’t 
want to have anything to do with them then. He is in the 
Student Health Service at the University of Toronto, and 
still is at age 70. 

CC: Maybe this is the time to comment on the family involve¬ 
ment at the Taylor Statten Camps — Ahmek and 
Wapomeo. Did this happen right from the beginning and 
how long did the family, the three children, Adele, Tay, 
and Page stay involved? 

AE: Well, Page and Tay didn’t become involved other than as 
regular staff members until after the War. 

CC: The second World War, 


12 




AE: Yes, both Tay and Page were overseas and Page, being the 
younger, has not had involvement in Camp except from the 
financial point of view. He did a lot of finances for the 
Board for the Taylor Statten Camps and he has always been 
Director of the September Camp. His son is the active 
Director of the September Camp and his daughter was in¬ 
volved too. So he hasn’t had the operation of the Boys’ 
Camp. After the War, Tay went down to Johns Hopkins 
and then he went to McGill. When he got his McGill 
appointment, it was on condition that he would have 3 
summer months off. After 1946 or ’47, he was able to be¬ 
come Director of Ahmek. In fact, I am not sure when Dad 
stopped and Tay started but there was a period when they 
were both running the show. 

CC: And you became Director of Wapomeo when? 

AE: I was always called Associate Director. I never called myself 
Director while mother was at all active and her activity was 
very slight. She always went over to the Camp and stayed 
all day but other than sit on the dock and talk to staff and 
work in the weavery, that was her . . . she never really par¬ 
ticipated in a leadership role as we consider a leader. She 
always had the great admiration and love of everyone. The 
kids just flocked to her, and she was a grandmother figure, 
I guess. They adored her, and I have lots of pictures of her 
sitting on the dock with kids hanging over her. 



CC: As Associate Director, when did you begin and how long 
did it continue? 

AE: My last summer was 1975 and I was really directing it when 
I came back from England in 1938,1 would say. 

CC: Whew, that’s a good stint. 

AE: That was long enough. 

CC: And your Mom passed away in . . .? 

AE: 1969. 

CC:. I was going to say the early ’70’s. I remember her attending 
a Society of Camp Directors meeting because she is one of 
the Charter members. 

AE: That’s right. She and Mary Hamilton and Mary S. Edgar 
were honorary members. 

CC: Speaking about the Society of Camp Directors, could we 
go to the beginnings of Camping Associations and the 
major role your Dad played in the formation of the OCA 
and CCA specifically? 

AE: Well, in the early 30’s there were regular meetings, mostly 
social — Edgar, Hamilton, Halliday, Chapman, Cochrane 
and Statten, those six. 


CC: Let’s stretch that out now. You are referring to Mary S. 
Edgar of Glen Bernard Camp, Mary G. Hamilton of Camp 
Tanamakoon, Ferna Halliday of Camp Oconto, Ernie 
Chapman of Camp Kagawong, A. L. Cochrane of Camp 
Temagami and your Father of the Taylor Statten Camps. 
Charlie Plewman wasn’t part of the group? 

AE: Not the first part, but he was very soon after that. Those 
six were the group that met. 

CC:. And Arnold Ward? 

AE: No. Arnold Ward was never . . . see, these are private 
Camp Directors and maybe because Arnold Ward was an 
agency Camp Director ... What Camp did he direct? 

CC: Well, I don’t know whether he ever directed a Camp. He 
was a President of the Ontario Camping Association but I 
am not sure he ever did direct a Camp. 

AE: Yes and he was on the National Council YMCA. He was on 
the staff at Ahmek when Dad brought in some great older 
men including David Lewis and Arnold Ward. His wife 
died up there, as a matter of fact... very sad. 

CC: That was during the second World War. 

AE: Yes. 

CC: The group of six had early meetings.... 

AE: These six people used to gather at people’s homes. I don’t 
know how often, I guess 4 or 5 times a year. As I say, a 
great deal of it was social and anything they talked about 
was sort of trivial in a way because they had secrets. No¬ 
body ever knew what anybody paid their staff, for instance. 
They never discussed salaries, and I can’t remember what 
they did discuss. I was secretary, I finally started to take 
notes sometime before I got married, and that was 1935. I 
used to attend the meetings. Bill Chapman was there, some¬ 
times too. Well, then the Dansons were the next people. 

CC: I was going to ask you about the Dansons. 

AE: They came in next. Sadie and Joe would come. Then 
Charlie Plewman, yes, at about the same time. 

CC: Our records show that the OCA became a reality in 1933 
and then the CCA became a reality in 1936. Do those dates 
sound right? 

AE: ’36 sounds early to me but 1 ... ’33 sounds right. De¬ 
pending on what you mean by the OCA. They opened their 
doors to agency camps. Edith Calver of Bolton was one of 
the early members, 1 know, and R. S. McLean of the 
Religious Council was an early member. 

CC: I read that your Dad helped with the formation of the 
Quebec Camping Association along with F. M. VanWagner 
in 1937. 

AE: Well that is why I thought the Canadian Camping Associ¬ 
ation was not until.... 

CC: After that had happened? 

AE: My impression was that it was 1938. 

CC: We may be celebrating 50 years under false pretenses, 
so let’s not upset that apple cart. 

AE: No, 50 years makes it ‘36. Well, I’ll buy that. VanWagner 
was President of Quebec but he wasn’t President of the 
Canadian Camping Association until way on because there 
was Taylor Statten and then there was Mary S. Edgar. Wait 
a minute, I am getting a little mixed up between my 
columns.... 

CC: I am not sure that Mary Edgar was ever President of the 
CCA. Dais Gass followed your Dad, then Anne Vail, Ted 
Yard, Irv Haladner and, then, F. M. VanWagner. 1 think 
that was the sequence. In the early ’40’s, your Dad became 
the President of the American Camping Association. This 
is fascinating because he was the only human being that 
has ever been President of the two National Associations. 


13 




AE: Right from the beginning, he was very active always on 
committees and as a speaker on ACA. Yon know the 
American Camping Association, originally, was the Camp 
Directors Association and they were all private Camp 
Directors. Taylor Statten and Mary S. Edgar were members 
of that in ‘24 or *25 and they used to go to meetings in the 
United States. We were always members of the ACA and, 
as I say, he was actively so. He had a great many very good 
friends. Jack Cheley was one of them. I am trying to think 
of the others... Walton Johnson, Frank Bell, Ted Cavins. 
They were all close friends of his. 

CC: Your Dad did so many other things that weren’t directly 
within the realm of camping, per se, that enriched the lives 
of people, particularly young people. Can we talk a little 
bit about some of those things? 

AE: Do you mean starting in days when he was formulating the 
Canadian Standard Efficiency Tests, for instance? 

CC: Yes, what are they? 

AE: It had partly to do with camping, I suppose. It had some 
areas in it but it was a standard, I always thought that it 
was created sort of in opposition to the Boy Scouts ... it 
had to do with young people, young men, not children but 
young men, and giving them leadership tools and skills. 
They were called Tuxis Boys. The Trail Rangers were the 
younger group that came along after. They started in about 
1917,1 think. 

CC: I always connected them with the United Church of Canada 
which of course didn’t start until 1925 ... 

AE: No, it wasn’t just the United Church but there were church 
people involved in it. There were Methodists and Congre- 
gatlonalists. Church of England was more Boy Scouts, 
wasn’t it? 

CC: C.S.E.T. wasn’t church-based? I kind of felt that CSET 
was church-based ... not YMCA. 

AE: Something like the CGIT, you mean. 

CC: Yes. 

AE: It was to a certain extent, but I don’t think as much as 
CGIT. It was YMCA as well as Church. It grew out of the 
National Council YMCA I think. 

CC: So, your Dad became involved when he was the National 
YMCA Boys Work Secretary. He wasn’t commissioned by 
any group to do it, he ... 

AE: It just grew out of that, I think, and along with this Sunday 
School leader group as well. That’s why there was a 
religious emphasis.... 

CC: Was the Boys’ Parliament a part of that? Did it go hand in 
glove with that? 

AE: Yes, I think so. This is something I would have to check 
into but it was all at the same time and it was leadership 
you see.... 

CC: Not necessarily camp leadership but... 

AE: Making better citizens. That was sort of the underlying 
theme . . . the fourfold way of life started then with Tuxis 
because of its significance, the cross in the middle which 
was Christ, you and I, Tuxis and . . . that was ... I said 
that Dad was an Evangelist and he really was, apparently. 
He didn’t have a religious background as a child, to any 
great extent. They were Methodists at Erindale. I must tell 
you a story about my great grandfather Emerson Taylor 
who was a Councillor and he was an important person in 
Erindale. He really ran everything pretty much his way and 
apparently the village no-good died. The only cemetery 
there was the one up on the hill which is at the Anglican 
Church in Erindale. And the Anglicans wouldn’t bury this 
man, so Emerson Taylor bought a plot of land, quite a big 
plot of land, on the other side of the fence beside the 
cemetery up on the hill, which I have seen . •. and arranged 


that this old boy would be buried up there, much to the 
horror of everyone else who was Anglican in town. As a 
result, that’s where my grandparents are buried, up on the 
other side of the fence... I think they have taken the fence 
down, mind you, but I was there about 15 years ago ... no 
it must have been more than that, about 20 years ago, and 
there was a verger mowing the lawn and I told him who I 
was. His father had been there and knew my father, and he 
showed me where my grandparents were buried . . . sup¬ 
posedly on the other side of the fence. 

CC: Your Dad had an active role as well in Service Clubs, didn’t 
he? 

AE: Yes, in 1920, who was the man who was in New York? 
... Atkinson? 

CC: C. J. Atkinson with the Boys’ Clubs of America? 

AE: Well C. J. Atkinson became involved in Rotary. He 
decided he wanted to spread this Boys’ Club influence and 
get some help, so he got the Rotary Club in New York in¬ 
volved in it... in the Boys’ Clubs ... and when there was 
an International Rotary Convention in 1922 in Atlantic 
City, he asked Taylor Statten to go and speak, and I was 
there. It was a tremendous Hall and that was when Dad 
became particularly involved in Rotary. He and C. J. 
Atkinson ... after that... travelled back and forth across 
Canada and went to 60 Rotary Clubs in 60 days, as well as 
nipping down into the States every once in a while. After 
that, he became a member of the Toronto Rotary Club and 
was very active in the Boys’ Committee and was a very 
good member. He went to Rotary in Huntsville in the 
summer and to Rotary in Florida in the winter. 

CC: And the Religious Education Council, what was that 
connection? 

AE: Well it was part ... it became connected with the Y men 
through the Boys* Work Board. The Canadian Boys’ Work 
Board was Religious Education Council and YMCA and 
they had their offices together on Queen Street in Toronto. 
There were two men I remember. I can only remember one 
of their names and that was R. S. MacLean and they were 
active in the Camping Association too in the early days. 
Dad was not a church-goer in his later years. Mother was 
much more so. We had a certain amount of religion in 
Camp. We always had Sunday Chapel services. We con¬ 
sidered ourselves non-denominational ... we were non- 
denominational and we always had a lot of Jewish campers. 
Chick Hendry was very critical of us because we didn’t 
light candles on Friday night. Occasionally, someone 
would become very enthusiastic about Communion and 
they would have somebody come in from Huntsville. The 
‘good old’ Anglicans would want to have some com¬ 
munion. And we would have a priest come in but we 
wouldn’t have anyone come in to celebrate Friday evenings. 
No one seemed to mind. I once asked an old Ahmek 
camper, Ken Rotenberg, why he didn’t send his daughter, 
Rebecca, to a Camp for Jewish children. He said, “Adele, 
I send her to Wapomeo because it is the best Camp.” Of 
course, that made me feel very good. 

CC: You could put that into your brochure. 

AE: Yes. 

CC: Now, when your Dad was involved at Pickering College, 
did it begin in connection with a church? 

AE: It’s Quaker, it has always been Quaker. It was Quaker 
when it was out at Pickering and it burned down. There 
were a number of years during the first War when there 
was no Pickering College. It didn’t start until 1927 in the 
new building up in Newmarket. It is very Quaker still. 

CC: Your Dad was an evangelist preacher in his younger days, 
and... 


14 



AE: Oh, he would be a good Quaker, too. He dropped that 
sort of outward flaunting of religion ... if he ever did it. 
I can’t imagine he did but, anyway, he must have to a 
certain extent. I think that the Quaker approach would be 
very much to his liking. 

CC: He was involved when his brother-in-law Wally Forgie 
established Camp Tonakela in India. 

AE: Yes, Wally went out to India after his wife died in Calgary 
in 1925, and he went out as a YMCA man. While he was 
out there, he saw so much that could be done that the Y 
wasn’t doing that eventually he drew away from the 
YMCA ... 

CC: Why wasn’t the YMCA doing it? 

AE: Well they were trying to be so Christian that it didn’t mix 
with the Hindu ... 

CC: And the purpose of the Y was to develop Christian person¬ 
alities in a Christian Society. 

AE: Apparently... 

CC: And it didn’t mix with Hinduism . .. 

AE: That was where Wally broke with the Y because he couldn’t 
expect the Y to change and Wally didn’t feel that trying 
to convert the Indians to Christianity was going to be any 
good at all. So Wally virtually became a Hindu and his 
burial was Hindu, too. He started the Camp just taking 
kids off the street, and when we were in India I could see 
how you could pick kids off the street... 

CC: In the city of Madras wasn’t it? 

AE: In the city of Madras, yes. I don’t know where his first 
property was exactly. The property we visited was 12 miles 
out of Madras and when Mother and Dad opened Camp 
Tonakela in 1938, it had been operating for a while before 
that. It wasn’t called Camp Tonakela. It became Tonakela 
when my parents went over. Wally decided to name it 
Tonakela. 

CC: It is interesting why he did that, isn’t it? 

AE: Well yes it is. Of course he was a great admirer of my 
mother, who was the sister of his beloved wife, and there 
was in the Tamil language a word that was “Tonakia” 
which meant “you first’’, and he thought this would be a 
very suitable name for Camp Tonakela. 

CC: But your mother’s Camp name was Tonakela wasn’t it? 

AE: Yes, it was Ojibway. 

CC: Which came first? 

AE: My mother’s name. She was named Tonakela. Oh when... 

I guess at the beginning of the Girls’ Camp. She was never 
called Mrs. Statten by anybody. 

CC: What was your camp name? 

AE: Couchi, starting at Camp Couchiching, that was a nick¬ 
name. 

CC: So, Tonakela and Couchi. 1 know your Dad was involved 
in School Board Administration and we talked earlier 
about the SOS program during the first World War. 

AE: I think he felt badly not being in the War and was very 
anxious to make sure that the people who were not overseas 
were making their contribution and this was one of the 
ways that the Y got the younger boys involved in War 
work. It was during the second World War ... we all 
worked for the Red Cross. The SOS was Soldiers of the 
Soil and it was young people . . . young men I think . . . 
only too young to go overseas and they worked on the 
farms. 

CC: Now he would be in his early 30’s at the end of the War in 
1918... maybe 36? 

AE: Yes... 36. 


CC: What a legacy he left for all of us. Very literally, everyone 
in Camping throughout North America followed his 
leadership, followed his innovations, followed the kind of 
person he was and the kind of Camp atmosphere he 
created. It is quite a legacy. Why do you suppose ...? 

AE: The time was right I guess we would say. He had some 
very powerful friends in the United States in Camping. I 
wish I could remember all the names other than Jack 
Cheley and Frank Bell and Walton Johnson and Ted 
Cavins and there were two or three others, Horace Kephart, 
and . . . there is another man who wrote a book . . . and I 
felt that they . . . influenced each other. I think that Dad 
learned a lot from them because they had a longer back¬ 
ground in organized camping than we had up here. As I 
say, he and Mary Edgar and Mother went, starting in 
1911, to these Camp Directors’ meetings before the 
American Camping Association really was started. And 
Dad attracted leaders. I think he made sure he had a 
swimming instructor, sailing instructor and riding in¬ 
structor, canoeing instructor. Of course, we had the 
wonderful Bill Stoqua as the canoeing instructor and I 
have a brochure to give you on that. Dad was not an 
athlete himself, like the people he had leading most de¬ 
partments, and the departments ... the areas he was most 
interested in were the arts and crafts and drama and music 
and he was a self-taught person in this regard. He en¬ 
joyed seeing young people participate and present them¬ 
selves in musicals and then of course, he could see that this 
influence was being passed over to the campers who came 
to listen to them and started to admire these performers. 
Crafts was an area that my Mother was very interested in 
and we developed wonderful crafts at Wapomeo. 



CC: It has been said that camping is North America’s number 
one contribution to the field of education and Taylor 
Statten was irrefutably the number one leader in camping. 
That had to be partially due to the things that happened 
at Camp Ahmek and Camp Wapomeo. What program 
features of the Taylor Statten Camps do you think were the 
biggest influences ... the kinds of emphasis from which 
you measure Taylor Statten Camps? 

AE: It is hard to say, there was a ... in all the sort of traditional 
camp things . . . there was a desire to have excellence. I 
don’t think that it was overdone. For instance, we had 
good people from RCYC doing the sailing. We had riders 
who were of Olympic calibre. In fact, we had one boy who 
couldn’t take any pay or he wouldn’t be able to go on the 
Olympic team after the summer. It appears that those 
things just happened because of our reputation. 

CC: A large number of programs that started in the Taylor 
Statten Camps were picked up by the rest of us . . . the 
canoeing program, and that huge fleet of canoes you had, 
the outtripping, the marvellous emphasis on nature and 
environmental education, Indian Council and all the aura 
it had surrounding it. Those programs didn’t just happen, 
did they? 


15 





AE: Well because of our location, certainly the environment 
and nature study, nature hikes, we used to have shields and 
instead of badges we had bars on these shields that would 
give you number 1 in sailing, number 2 in nature and so on 
and so forth, and there was a lot of emphasis in the early 
days put on getting grades. That changed when our pro¬ 
gram became less stylized. I remember, as a camper, there 
were things that we had to do . . . certainly in the 30’s there 
was a psychologist, and who was the psychologist . . . 
Dewey? His educational approach influenced Forest Hill 
School for instance, and I think that influence came into 
the Camp because all the silver cups were put away . . . and 
the crests ... the shields stopped in the late 20’s or early 
30’s I guess. Things became much more relaxed and there 
was much more opportunity to sit on a rock and think and 
Dad’s idea of canoetripping was “smoothing it while you 
rough it.” He didn’t like people to just go out and be 
tough. He liked people to enjoy what they did and take 
time to listen and appreciate the sunsets and so on. 

CC: Did it really happen that way? That is quite a philosophical 
statement, you know. 

AE: He tried in every way he could to do that, and one of the 
greatest influences, daily influences, were his morning 
meditations which he did himself day after day after day. 
They were, I suppose, five minutes and they were always 
sort of the same thought with a different twist. 

CC: There was always a moral to his story? 

AE: Practically always a moral, yes I think it was Hedley 
Dimock that started the TOF “the other fellow,” but that 
sort of continued on through. After the meditation people 
would, and still do I think, put their heads on the table 
and listen to music and the music was usually violins, some¬ 
times cello, the piano was too jiggly. The strings were much 
more soothing. Some of the kids went to sleep as a matter 
of fact. I remember having a pianist at Wapomeo ... I 
guess we didn’t have a violinist that year . . . that was suit¬ 
able anyway . . . Agnes Butcher was playing for us and 
somebody said to me, “Oh can’t you get her to play some¬ 
thing less lilty and less dancy and more meditative after 
morning meditation?” We were starting morning medi¬ 
tation at Wapomeo too. So I spoke to Agnes and said “Do 
you know something a little more serious and sober?” The 
next morning she played the Funeral March and, from then 
on, we liked her better. We decided she at least had a sense 
of humour. Dad always loved the theatre and I think this is 
why the Council Ring because it was a spectacle and ... 

CC: It was a Ceremony. 

AE: And it was a Ceremony, yes. It was always done very 
precisely, very organized, and well planned. Some of us 
were in fear and trembling that somebody would do the 
wrong thing and spoil the atmosphere ... 

CC: There were certain rituals that were done at every Council 
Ring every time? 

AE: Yes, the beginning and ending were always the same and 
most inspirational. 

CC: If we had been able to interview your Dad today, what do 
you suppose his closing remarks would be if we were to 
ask him “What were the joys of camping to you, what do 
you recall as being the highlights of your career?” 

AE: Well I am sure that it was his association with young 
people that kept him going. He liked people of all kinds 
and of all ages; he had a great circle of friends. And after 
he became inactive at Camp, he organized things in his 
group down in Florida. But I think he really was great in 
his heyday . . . mind you I could see it dropping off during 
his latter years. There wasn’t the same sort of sparkle of 
enthusiasm, as there had been at his height. As I think 
back, he would paddle across the lake every morning for 


years before he got a motor boat. I can just see him going 
off and probably planning his day and having that few 
minutes to himself as he paddled across. Setting up goals 
for himself and his campers. He was always reaching and 
expected other people to do the same. 

CC: Reaching for ...? 

AE: Something better. Reaching for the stars, maybe. I don’t 
know. 

CC: Not only did he reach, he grasped many. 

AE: Yes, he had fun in him, too. He wasn’t all serious. 

CC: Must have been that P.T. Barnum “gene” at work. 

AE: Yes, yes. He used to always think that he had to have 
something every summer that was different whether it 
would be the fact that he got goats wandering around the 
Camp until they got too frisky. What other things did he 
have, did he do? Nothing stood in his way, we had all the 
small sketches of Tom Thompson come from the National 
Gallery. Now, whoever arranged that I am not sure, I 
wasn’t involved enough to know. We had these Tom 
Thompson sketches from 1932 or ’33 brought over from 
Ottawa and we carried them up to the Tom Thompson 
Totem. 



CC: Why was there a Tom Thompson Totem? 

AE: Well, he was drowned up there. 

CC: When? 

AE: 1917, in Canoe Lake, Tom Thompson was drowned, so his 
ghost still paddles up and down the lake on the anniversary 
of when his body was surfaced. 

CC: Your family had been going to Camp throughout that time, 
or at least camping on Canoe Lake, but the Taylor Statten 
Camps hadn’t started quite yet. . . in 1917. 

AE: Tom Thompson helped to build the fireplace. Chubby 
knew Tom Thompson and Charlie Plewman knew Tom 
Thompson . . . helped to carry' his casket up the hill as a 
matter of fact. But he was drowned in July of 1917 and we 
didn’t ever go up to Canoe Lake until September so we 
were not there at the time. Tom Thompson has always been 
a very’ important person in that part of the woods and I 
think that’s the reason that art . . . that Dad encouraged 
artists to come up and a lot of the young men who became 
pretty good painters always felt they had been influenced 
by Tom Thompson. 

CC: How do you suppose your Dad felt about passing on this 
great tradition of the Taylor Statten Camps to Tay and to 
you? Did he ever say anything to you? 

AE: Well I think he found it difficult, not to me because I was 
running my show separately. I think he found it difficult to 
see Tay taking over and Tay’s methods not being his 
methods. I think he found that difficult and I think that is 
why he sort of .... 

CC: Hung on ... ? 


16 




No, dropped out. You know ... sort of ... completely. He 
hung on for a while but he gave up to Tay ... or handed 
over to Tay I should say. I think it was a very difficult 
period, because he had been the Big Chief and his word 
was law and all these wonderful people that he had up there 
cow-towed to him, except Ernest Thompson Seton who 
would cow-tow to nobody and I wouldn’t say that Jack 
Miner would either. Not that Chick, and Alex and Hedley 
would either but they were great admirers of the Chief. 


He certainly was the Big Chief. He was the Chief to many 
of us in camping and we are not only the beneficiaries of all 
that he stood for in camping, but we have been very proud 
of his accomplishments ... yet I am sure not any more so 
than you have been. 

No, I have been amazed though too. I still meet people who 
well remember, or their fathers were closely involved, and it 
is a great joy to meet them and hear people speak highly of 
him. He certainly meant an awful lot to our family. 

And to the camping family. 



A PERSONAL NOTE 

For the past twenty years I have concentrated my thought 
and energy on assisting boys in character development. Very 
early I learned that a boys’ character was most affected during 
his leisure time. This is because of the enthusiasm with which 
he throws himself into the things he wants to do. 

Character is contagious. 11 is caught, not taught. Expose 
a boy during his leisure time to men of sterling character 
and he will quickly acquire similar characteristics. 

A properly supervised summer camp provides the variety of 
experiences which every normal boy enjoys, together with the 
social contacts needed in developing strong manly character 

Camp Ahmek is the culmination of my aim to create a 
character-building centre permeated with an atmosphere which 
would inspire boys to develop the best that is in them. 

At Camp Ahmek we have surrounded the boys with the 
creative force of positive suggestion. We have eliminated 
the word “don’t’’ and have substituted incentives and motives 
for purposeful activity. Through the influence of good music 
of strong personalities, of the happy smile and the inspiring 
story, every boy soon catches “The Ahmek Spirit.” 

By admitting a limited number of boys I am able to 
give my personal attention where it is needed. The 
testimony of parents who have entrusted their shy and 
backward boys to my care is most encouraging. 

The following pages will give some idea of Camp Ahmek, but 
it is only by visiting the camp and breathing its atmosphere and 
feeling its influence that the spirit of Camp Ahmek is revealed. 

TAYLOR STATTEN. 


17

The information below is your invitation to an historic and invaluable exchange on camping views. This 2nd International 
Camping Congress will address the challenges facing all of us in camping today. The Canadian Camping Association will be making 
major contributions at this Congress and, in turn, stands to benefit greatly from the opportunities it can provide. 

Programs for this Congress have been grouped into six streams: Program; Marketing and Public Relations; Business, Finance, 
Operations; Personnel; Support Services and Whom We serve. 

In each of the streams there will be offered six-hour seminars, three-hour workshops and one-and-one-half hour interest 
sessions. At any given time there will be up to 30 sessions from which to choose. 

The fee for the Congress is $200.00 US for early registration (as compared to the later $260.00 US). This early registration fee can 
be guaranteed with a $50.00 US deposit. Spousal registrations are half price. Special airfares from Toronto have been arranged with 
U.S. AIR. The return ticket is $250.00 Cdn. (as compared to the regular $390.00 Cdn.). As an extra benefit the tickets down are 
valid from March 2-6, 1987 and they are open ended. This allows families to fly down to Washington late in the Congress week for 
a family vacation to follow the event. 

Following the initial registration and deposit a detailed registration form is sent. Please note that the steering committee has set up 
a channelling system for the donation portion of the final payment. Donations made from Canada can return to Canadians. 

Rates at the Shoreham Hotel are approximately $80.00 U.S./night. Accommodation at the nearby 4H Club Conference Centre is 
$20 - $25.00 U.S./night (includes breakfast). 

More details are on their way to you. In the meantime, mark calendars and ear mark funds for this important camping event.

Second International Camping Congress

1806 Avenue Road, Suite 2, Toronto, Ontario M5M3Z1
