The Second International Camping Congress will be held on March 2- 5, 1987, at the Shoreham Hotel in Washington, D.C., 
U.S.A. The Congress is jointly sponsored by the American Camping Association, Canadian Camping Association, and Jamaica 
Camping and Hiking Association and the National Camping Association of Japan. Camping leaders throughout the world will be 
present to bring their concerns about elements to our “Fragile World” which challenge the organized camping, environmental and 
experiential education community to impact participants for future action. 

Specifically, the Congress shall seek to share current knowledge and techniques in organized camping and outdoor environmental 
and experiential education; consider global issues such as peace and conservation which can be impacted by the outdoor experience 
movement; explore with a global perspective the future trends of the camping, outdoor environmental and experiential education 
movements and their implication on culture and foster an atmosphere of personal sharing across international and interdisciplinary 
lines. 

Speakers: We’re pleased to announce the Congress will be opened by the internationally acclaimed group “Up With People” who 
have entertained millions of people around the world; Pete Seeger, internationally known for his folk writing and his dedication and 
commitment to the environment; William Penn Mott, the U.S. National Park Service Director who has been described as “one of 
the most widely respected conservationists in America and the World”; and former ambassador to the U.S.A. and U.S.S.R. from 
India, T. N. Kaul whose world interests on behalf of India has given him the acclaim of World Statesman. 

The Congress has the support and cooperation of the following: Alliance for Environmental Education of the U.S.A.; American 
Alliance for Health, Physical Education, Recreation and Dance (AAHPERD); American Nature Study Society; Association for 
Experiential Education; Boy Scouts of America; Boys’ Clubs of America; Camping Association of South Australia; Canadian 
Youth Science Foundation; Christian Camping International, U.S. Division; Cooperative Extension Service: 4-H; Council of 
Outdoor Educators of Ontario, Canada; European YMCA Camping Group; Girl Scouts of the U.S.A.; International Association 
of Conference Center Administrators; Jewish Welfare Board; National Board of YWCA of the U.S.A.; National Park and 
Recreation Association of the U.S.A.; National Society for Internships and Experiential Education of the U.S.A.; World Alliance 
of YMCAs; the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts; and YMCA of the U.S.A. 






UNDER OPEN SKIES 


A CAMP RECIPE 

by Mary S. Edgar 

A lake-bowl of water, hill-rimmed and blue 
Sprinkle with sunshine, diffused through and through 
Flavouring from miles of evergreen trees 
Stir altogether with clear northern breeze. 

Add a flash of white wings, the dash of a brook 
Or a slow-dropping stream from a fern-hidden nook. 

Allure all the children from all kith and kin. 

And after much sorting, and much merry din 
Place them in cabins where each has a friend. 

Provide them with fun and some leisure to spend. 

Season with crafts, with sailing and trips. 

With riding and tennis, canoeing and dips. 

Toast by a fire, or bake in the sun 
Until every camper is perfectly done. 

Keep them in safety eight weeks, or till brown: 

Then they are ready to serve back in town. 

REPRINTED FROM CANADIAN 
CAMPING MAGAZINE, DEC. 1960. 

Welcome to our regular feature entitled Under Open Skies. The 
beautiful poem above, A CAMP RECIPE, was written by Mary 
S. Edgar, an Honourary President of the Canadian Camping 
Association, and the Founder of Canadian Camping Magazine. 
With a tribute in our hearts to Mary, we begin this regular feature 
of our CCA/ACC Magazine. 

Camp is a wonderful place for spiritual growth — services, 
ceremonies and quiet times conducted in the out-of-doors create 
memories that last forever, and many of us still cherish the 
poems, spiritual songs and sermonettes that we experienced at 
Camp. 

We invite all our readers to contribute their own bits of 
inspiration whether they are poems, thoughts for the day, 
prayers, or sermonettes. Please send your contributions to the 
Canadian Camping Magazine, R.R. #1, Huntsville, Ontario, 
POA 1K0, and we will re-print them in our Under Open Skies 
feature. 

We would invite, firstly, the original and creative works of our 
own members but if your items are reprinted from another source 
then please include that source for reference.

A PRAYER FOR LEADERS 

Lord of all learning and leaders, 

At best we blunder along 
While ours is the honour to forge out ahead, 

A daring and pioneer throng. 

Too easily sure and contented 
With successes of yesterdays, 

While Youth has the untried Tomorrow 
Calling to untrodden ways. 

May all of our short-comings shame us 
Till we learn to be humble and wise, 

Ready as seers and as prophets 
To lift up eager young eyes. 

Tis not our task to furnish and mind 
But to fan a flame in the soul, 

Sending them forth with a will and a dream 
To their high and potential goal. 

Give us, O Lord of all leaders 
A sense of our sacred task, 

The equipment needed to face it 
And a blessing, we humbly ask. 

— Mary S. Edgar 

REPRINTED FROM CANADIAN 
CAMPING MAGAZINE, APRIL 1967. 


IMMIGRATION INFORMATION 

Camps across Canada owe thanks to Barry Lowes, Chairman 
of C.C.A/s Immigration Task Force. Many Canadian camping 
people are aware of the concerns we had regarding medicals for 
foreign camp counsellors. The news was gloomy until Barry and 
his committee of Joe Kronick and Ben Wise met with the 
Honourable Jake Epp, Minister of Health and Welfare Canada. 
That April 22nd meeting resulted in the following amendments: 

The Minister has agreed to amend the procedures as follows: 

1. Foreign camp counsellors will now obtain the Ministry’s 
Medical Form MS 1017 from the nearest Consulate. 

They can telephone or go in person. 

We are also working on a plan to have CCA/ACC provide 
them directly to camps. For now, advise counsellors to ob¬ 
tain it from the nearest Consulate. 

2. The counsellor has the medical form completed by his own 
doctor. 

3. The counsellor brings the completed medical form to the 
border, plus a photocopy for the camp, together with his/ 
her other Immigration papers. The officer at the border will 
take the original medical form and send it to Ottawa. 

4. The counsellor once he has the medical form from the 
Consulate, has no need to go back to or deal further with 
the Consulate. Just fill out the medical form and bring it to 
the border. 

This new protocol simplifies greatly the process of gaining entry 
into Canada. 

Over the past several years, Barry has been working hard on 
our behalf as our liaison with the Federal Government. We salute 
you, Barry Lowes, for the time and effort you have given to 
ensure better camping for everyone. 

If CCA/ ACC camps have any questions, concerns or problems 
regarding foreign camp counsellors, please call Barry at 
416-653-2118, or after June 20 at 705-457-2813.

HERE IS YOUR CHALLENGE, 
O, COUNSELLOR! 



This article is based on the talk pre¬ 
sented by Mrs. Ebbs at the Ontario Camp¬ 
ing Association Annual Conference, 
March 1965. 


VOICE VOTRE DEFI, CONSEILLER 

Cet article est basd sur un discours 
prdsentd par Mme Ebbs a la con¬ 
ference annuelle de ^association des 
camps de /'Ontario mars 1965. Dans 
cet article elle raconte les souvenirs 
de sa jeunesse et elle identifie le 
campeur comme la raison d’etre du 
conseiller. Les besoins des campeurs 
sont vdritables et le conseiller peut y 
satisfaire seulement avec beaucoup 
d’effort. Les recompenses au con¬ 
seiller sont heureusement vdritables 


A shocker to me, if not to you, is that I 
have been camping for a little over fifty 
years, that’s half a century! During that 
time there have been changes, but there 
are many similarities in camping then and 
now, and in the opportunities and re¬ 
sponsibilities awaiting the new counsellor. 
The more background you can get for this 
job, the more you are going to feel “at 
home” with it. 

Let me reminisce a little, and perhaps 
this will stir memories for you too. I 
remember my first portage (apparently a 
very short one) when I struck out ahead 
of my parents, then 1 went back to them, 
still with my pack on my back, to inform 
them the pack was too heavy —thus, in 
fact, covering the portage twice! Only 
once did 1 have a fear of drowning, this 
while crossing an open bay in a high wind 
when I was middle man in the canoe. The 
only scar I carry is on one finger when I 


by A dele Ebbs, 

Director, Camp Wapomeo for Girls 
Taylor Statten Camps 


carelessly opened a can of sardines and 
part of my finger with it. The latter was 
stuck back on quickly and taped up by my 
smart counsellor. 

I remember: a family of otters sur¬ 
rounding our canoes at dusk once— 
hissing . . ., I remember when we found a 
heronry and one of the girls climbed a 
pine tree and got wonderful pictures of 
those balls of fluff in their huge nest. I 
remember many beaver dams, which were 
a nuisance to lift our canoes and gear 
over, but which were of equal use to 
beavers and trippers, because we had 
water to paddle in. And there was the time 
we met a bear cub on a portage who just 
sat and stared, while we wondered 
uneasily where mama bear was. I 
remember being disturbed one night while 
sleeping in my bag under the stars — a 
persistent rustling just near my head — oh, 
it couldn’t have been anything but a 
mouse. I tried to ignore it, then took my 
flashlight from under my pillow and 
shone it into the eyes of a startled 
skunk —or, which of us do you think was 
the more startled? 

A counsellor is at heart a camper 

If you are lucky enough to be able to get 
away from civilization, these things 
haven’t changed. But our “frontiers’’ are 
coming closer with their accessibility by 
road. You used to be able to bicycle out 
into the country for picnics; now you have 
to drive or go by bus to reach the country. 
But there are good areas being saved by 
our Conservation Authorities. Neverthe¬ 
less with recreational areas being made 
accessible, our country is opened up for 
tourism. This is an ever increasing 
challenge to campers. We have to know 
and practise conservation. As counsellors 
we must cherish and share the thrill and 
excitement of our great out-of-doors, so 
that this won’t be lost to the next 
generation. It is really no task to learn 
more about nature, so long as you 
continue to be curious about the un¬ 
known, alert to its magic, and you 
develop attitudes, interests and habits 
related to the wise use of resources. 

We want to be campers, and to me this 
means a fundamental desire to be in the 
out-of-doors: in the woods, on a high hill, 
by a lake or a creek, or in the sugar- 
bush of a friendly farmer. We don’t mind 
the weather —if it’s hot, we avoid the dis¬ 
comforts of sunburn at the same time 


getting a healthy tan. If it’s wet and cold, 
we wear the proper gear and become more 
active. We know there’ll be black flies the 
end of June and in early July, we know 
we’ll be pursued by mosquitoes and deer 
flies, so we dress for them and fight them! 

Your first season as a counsellor 

You are looking forward to being coun¬ 
sellors this summer. You are on the verge 
of becoming “the older generation’’ in the 
eyes of your campers. But you are all 
young enough to have the strength, the 
imagination, the vision, the courage, to 
give to your camps and campers 
leadership in programming and 
community living which can make this 
summer more exciting and worthwhile 
than any they have ever had. 

You can still remember your excite¬ 
ment at doing things for the first time: 
becoming water-borne with your first 
stroke as you learned to swim, paddling a 
canoe in a straight line, moulding a 
creation from some clay or carving it from 
a piece of wood, finding a bird’s nest and 
then going back regularly to peek and see 
if the eggs had hatched. Discovering 
things for yourself for the first time is so 
thrilling. Today’s “organized” children 
need this release and time for these ex¬ 
plorations. Maybe you too have suffered 
from a highly organized routine. Maybe 
this summer will be the first time when 
you can really do some thinking for your¬ 
self, so don’t crowd your programme or 
that of your campers. 

Do you understand the needs of your 
campers? 

There are some needs so basic that you 
simply must remember them. To make it 
easier, memorize the code-word 
R.E.A.P.S., and the need represented by 
each letter. 

RECOGNITION — In leaving the 
family circle, the camper needs to find his 
place in the camp family—he needs to 
have a part to play in the group, be it an 
activity group or his cabin group — and to 
get approval for acceptable behaviour. 

EXPERIENCE (NEW) — Adventure, 
excitement, time to explore — so let the 
camper have time to go fishing without a 
hook if he wants, time to watch the sun set 
or to catch a snake. 

AFFECTION — and this isn’t just for 
little girls. We are too inclined to treat 


20 








children as “little adults”. Don’t forget 
that little boys need understanding and 
gentleness — they can’t always fight back 
and “be a man”. 

POWER — campers want to achieve, 
but let it be at their level. Having put forth 
effort, they should then have some 
feelings of success and mastery. 

SECURITY —realize what a sudden 
change it is for your campers from home 
to camp: new faces, and so many more 
people than at home, no city con¬ 
veniences, sharing one’s “bedroom” with 
several others, strange night noises, 
different food, and so on. 

All these children are at different stages 
of development especially with relation to 
camp activities. Find out the level of 
ability of each one as soon as you can, and 
then help to make goals for each indi¬ 
vidual. 

The job of a counsellor is real work 

Some people make work out of play 
and some play out of work. We belong to 
the second category. We strive to create a 
holiday atmosphere, at the same time 
realizing the seriousness of our task. 
Counselling at camp this summer may be 
your first job. How lucky you are to work 
in a permissive and sympathetic atmos¬ 
phere. Your camp director knows that 
you are serious in your desire to work, 
but also realizes that there must be some¬ 
thing more in it for you. Your education is 
continuing. This will be a growing-up 
experience because you will have to put 
your job first and your personal problems 
second. It will be harder to work with 
some than others, but you can’t always 
choose your cabin-mate or trip-mate, and 
so you will learn to get along with all kinds 
of people. 

There is dignity in having a job at a 
summer camp. More money can be made 
(and spent) waitressing at a lodge or doing 
highway construction. But counselling has 
an important social meaning — you get the 
feeling that you are needed by others, that 
you are playing an important role in the 
lives of others. You are not just a leader, 
you are a counsellor , and in this you have 
an advantage over the camper’s parents in 
your opportunity to help him develop. 

Even in the South Seas where we say 
that no one has to work, this is really a 
fantasy because a woman there judges the 
worth of a man by, for instance, his skill 
as a fisherman. 

You will be chosen for staff because of 
your individual attributes. Set your 
standards and goals and stick by them. 
Your contribution will be the greater if it 
is different from others on the staff. We 
are growing fortunate in Canada these 
days because we have young people not 
only from pioneer Canadian stock but 
also from other countries. If your cultural 
background is different, you can make a 


fine contribution by enriching various 
programmes with stories, songs, dances 
and costumes. You have an important job 
which is going to influence every child 
with whom you come in contact. It is 
wonderful to read about the influence 
young people are having abroad through 
C.U.S.O. and the Peace Corps. This is for 
a very few, and no more important than 
the tremendous job to be done in our 
camps this summer. 

It takes many qualities and skills to 
make a good counsellor. It would be an 
asset to be a Master of Social Work or a 
trained psychologist, and perhaps as a 
result of your camping experience with 
children and people in general, you might 
enter one of these fields in your higher 
education. In the meantime you are not a 
“pro”, so when you run into difficult 
situations, treat the individual as a human 



This story has been reprinted from the 
personal notes of Taylor Statten. One of 
his cherished responsibilities was a daily 
story-for-thought in the form of a 
Meditation. The boys at Camp Ahmek in 
Algonquin Park would gather round him 
quietly and listen as he began .... 

One evening at the early turn of the 
century I was in the locker room 
preparing to go on the gym floor when the 
fellow who had the locker next to mine 
came in. I was glad to see him. He was a 
member of our famous relay team and I 
wanted to hear about the big race in 
Buffalo held on the previous Saturday 
night. The sporting page of the Monday 
morning paper had featured it but now I 
could get it first hand. 

George said “You know I was more 
than anxious that we should win the race. 
I not only wanted to help bring the piece 


being, show him you really care, and listen 
to his problems. So much can be accom¬ 
plished by talking things out to a sympa¬ 
thetic listener. You too will find oppor¬ 
tunities to talk with your colleagues and 
supervisors, and do some personal 
planning for the future. If you can be 
receptive to others — reach out — share — 
give of yourself—this is what will make 
for a successful summer. And when you 
sit down to evaluate it, you will find that 
mutual sympathy and generosity of spirit 
make up the secret of true happiness. 

The counsellor’s job is a demanding 
one. It can’t be taken lightly, but the 
rewards are there. You’ll see them in the 
smiling face of a camper, the comrade¬ 
ship of your fellow staff, and the warm 
handshake of your camp director which 
will mean “Thanks. Well done!” 


of silverware back to Canada, but when 
they told me that I had been chosen to run 
the last relay, I was determined that we 
should win. I wondered who would run 
the last relay for the United States and 
when I read in the paper that it was to be 
the mighty Bonhog, I got cold shivers up 
and down my spine because I knew that 
Bonhog could run those 2 laps in that 
Buffalo Armories a trifle over a second 
faster than I, provided he was feeling fit. 

The first thing I did when we reached 
the dressing room in Buffalo was to look 
up Bonhog and then he said ‘I never felt 
better. I think that tonight I am going to 
beat my previous times.’ 

“I then knew that I could finish ahead 
of Bonhog only if the third relay runner 
gave me at least a second head start.” I sat 
there fascinated while George told me 
about the races. He said “The gong 
sounded in the dressing room and both 
teams went up to the track. The Canadian 
team entered the arena first and were 
given a good round of applause, but when 
the United States team came on the floor 
the greeting was tumultous. 

“They all moved over to the starting 
post to receive instructions and soon the 
first pair of runners took their positions 
on the track. The Canadian was given a 
silk Lion Ensign and the United States 
runner a silk Stars and Stripes. They were 
to run two laps and pass their flags on to 
the second pair of relay runners. 

“The Starter called on your mark — 
get set, and cracked his pistol and they 
were off. They ran neck and neck around 
the bend and kept together down the back 
stretch but as they rounded the far end 
our Canadian began to force his way 
ahead and a cheer went up from the group 
of Toronto and Hamilton fans who had 
gone over to Buffalo on the special train. 


RELAY RACE 


Cont’d on next page ... 

21 






I kept yelling ‘Go it old man, go it. A little 
more steam. That’s what I need to win 
this race’. 

“Down the stretch they came, the 
United States runner still trailing by a 
narrow margin, but our Canadian was 
little more than holding his lead. ‘I’ll 
need more than that to beat Bonhog.’ As 
they went down the back stretch the 
United States runner put on a sprint. This 
brought that Buffalo crowd to their feet in 
a cheering frenzy, but it did not last long 
and as the runners came down the stretch 
our second runner for Canada got his flag 
a split second before the United States 
runner grasped his and away they tore. As 
they rounded the bend the United States 
runner seemed to be closing in. From the 
cheering it was evident that he was gaining 
on our Canadian but as they neared the 
end of the back stretch the noise gradually 
subsided. The gap between the two 
runners slowly widened as they passed 
down the home stretch for the first lap I 
was tense with excitement. I was yelling 
‘Atta boy, atta boy, keep going that’s 
what I need. Just a little more, a little 
more and we have it in the bag.* 

“Around the bend, into the back 
stretch with our Canadian steadily 
increasing the lead and our Canadian 
contingent shouting their heads off. I 
could see that we now had the second I 
needed, but could we hold it. 

“Out stepped the third pair of runners 
and as our big Canadian took his place 
again I got the cold shivers. This was the 
young runner who less than a week ago, 
here in this dressing room told me he was 
a natural runner who didn’t need much 
training and that he was going up to the 
drug store to have an ice cream soda. His 
parting shot was, ‘I can beat the legs off 
you without training’. Now he was to 
have his first big race in senior company. 

There he crouched, in perfect form, 
alert, with outstretched arm, he grasped 
the Canadian flag and off he went, 
running like a deer. The United States 
runner got his flag and was away after 
him. Could our big Canadian hold that 
lead. Could he hold it? He was 
lengthening it. Down the back stretch they 
went. Our Canadians shouting them¬ 
selves hoarse, ‘nice going, nice going’. 
‘We now have more than I need, 
Bonhog can never catch me with a lead 
like that’. Our Canadian flashed past the 
starting line on the first lap of the home 
stretch quickly followed by the United 
States runner and as I stepped out to get 
into position to receive the flag on the 
next lap, suddenly I was aware of a change 
in the cheering. The shouting from our 
Canadians was weakening, that from the 
Buffalo crowd increasing and as I 
straightened up and gazed across to the 
other side of the track I could see that our 
big Canadian’s pace was slackening. The 


United States runner was digging in. Our 
big fellow was beginning to wobble. The 
United States runner was closing the gap. 
The cheering was louder and louder. Our 
runners feet seemed to be getting mixed 
up, now Buffalo was raising the roof. The 
Canadian made a desperate effort as the 
other man came abreast of him and then 
amidst a mighty outburst from that vast 
crowd the little United States runner 
passed our big Canadian. When it came to 
my turn to run the last relay, Bonhog had 
the Stars and Stripes and was away before 
me. Although I ran in the best time I ever 
made on that Buffalo track, what was the 
use.” 

The Race had been lost in the 3rd relay. 
George was highly wrought up over that 
race and I couldn’t get it out of my mind. 
After I got into bed that night I kept 
thinking about it. Suddenly I recalled an 
address I had heard recently in which the 
speaker said that our leaders undergo a 
complete change every 7 years. 

I know that I must have a new set of 
finger nails in less than seven years. They 
keep growing and I keep filing them 
down. I don’t know how long it takes to 
have a new set. 

My hair keeps growing. The barber 
keeps cutting it. I don’t know how long it 
takes to get a new head of hair. 

After a sun bath and a hot shower, a 
vigorous rub will remove a very thin layer 
of outer skin. I don’t know how long it 
takes to get a new hide. 

They say that within 7 years every bone, 
muscle, brain cell, in fact, every part of 
our body is completely changed. If that is 
true isn’t life like a long relay race. 

At birth we are given a name to carry 
instead of a flag and at the end of each 7 
year period we pass that name on to the 
next relay runner. I then said to myself, 
“Is there any relay that seems more 
important than the others. Back in these 
early days of my work with boys we did 
not know much about the importance of 
the early childhood year. We did, 
however, have statistics to prove that the 
period between 14 and 21, the third relay 
period was the time when most of the 
great life decisions were made. We could 
produce charts showing that the high 
point in the curve of religious conversions 
was between 14 and 16 years of age. That 
the great majority of vocational decisions 
as well as matrimonial choices were made 
in the late teens. I then said to myself if I 
can get a group of teen age boys to be still 
and do some serious thinking I shall try 
to help them picture for themselves that 
fellow who is going to run their next relay. 

Can you see him waiting there on your 
21st birthday eager to carry that name you 
are about to pass on? How he would 
appreciate a little head start! 

What are you going to give him? 


Will his be that sad lament of my friend 
George. “Oh you 3rd relay runner why 
didn’t you train? Why did you waste so 
much precious time? What chance have I 
in this race of life. How can I win with 
such a discouraging handicap?” 

No that is not what he will say. Not if 
you are one of the thousands of Canadian 
teen age boys who have heard this story of 
the Relay Race and have decided to go 
into serious training, who are keeping 
before them a mental picture of that 
fourth relay runner. Can’t you see him 
waiting there at 21, bright and alert, full 
of confidence, ready to say, as you hand 
your name on. “Thanks a lot. I appreciate 
what you have done for me. You with¬ 
stood many a strong temptation and have 
brought me a set of wholesome habits. I 
know it has not been easy going. You 
have stood the test against terrific 
pressure. That senior matric was a tough 
grind. The chances are I shall never have 
to face a more severe test. Now I am away 
to a good start and I shall do my best to 
pass this name on to the next relay runner 
with at least as good a head start as you 
have given me.” 

Taylor Statten 


Cette histoire a 6t6 reimprim6e des

Une de ses responsabilites cheries 
etait une histoire quotidienne sous

Cet homme doit se charger des defis 
de la vie aprfes avoir perdu sa

22 




There are four general principles of 
learning that are easily approached 
through Trials Walking. These principles 
apply to most human activity, but like all 
general principles their meaning becomes 
clearer as we see and experience their 
operation in specific situations. These 
principles are: 

Practice is necessary to develop and 
maintain skills. The movements and 
judgements involved in Trials Walking 
can be demanding and varied. The only 
way to get “good” at is is to practice. A 
little bit of initial practice will usually 
result in obvious improvements in 
routine moves. More difficult moves 
require considerable exploration and 
practice. A good course will involve a 
large variety of very different kinds of 
movement, problems, helping to 
establish a need to “get in shape” by 
practicing a variety of skills. 

Studying and planning help to solve 
new problems. Each section is a new 
and unique problem to be solved. Noth¬ 
ing exactly like it would probably have 
been encountered before, so it is useful 
to study it carefully (reconnaissance), 
and plan some moves in advance. (This 
is permitted, even encouraged, in 
Trials Walking. Participants may take 
as much time as they wish to look over 
a section by walking along outside the 
markers). 

We learn much about possible diffi¬ 
culties and solutions by watching 
others. People watching is one of the 
two most basic and pervasive methods 
of human learning. In Trials Walking 
there is no set order to walk the 
sections, people go when they are 
ready. If there are any doubts about 
how to handle a section it is very useful 
to watch others. 

We learn about our abilities and how to 
change them by accepting and thinking 
about our failures and successes. 
Analysis of our experience is the other 
basic and pervasive method of human 
learning. Anger and frustration are 
barriers to analysis, and unless people 
can accept their mistakes they will not 
learn from them. Likewise, excessive 
pride of accomplishment can blind us to 
the reasons for our success and set us up 
for a series of failures. A good Trials 
Walking course provides experience of 
success and failures for everybody. 

These four principles of learning apply 
to just about everything we do, but of 
course we will not know about them 
unless we are reflecting or looking for 
patterns in our experience, and we will not 
be able to use them to help us to better 
control our own learning unless we 
practice using them. 

Reflective Recreation involves an 
awareness beyond the immediate activity. 
It requires a larger perspective on 


learning, powers and self. These larger 
perspectives can be encouraged through 
timely discussion of the principles 
outlined here, showing how their 
application influences Trials Walking 
performance by pointing out specific 
examples. These same principles can then 
be discussed in any other learning 
situation, whether it be learning to spell, 
fly airplanes, or carry on a relationship 
(for example, much of our reading and 
conversation is a form of “watching 
others” where we learn how they handle 
various problems and opportunities). 

These four are not the only principles 
that could be identified, nor are they 
expressed in any final and authoritative 
way. In doing Reflective Recreation 
people should feel free to analyze, dig, or 
construct in whatever way is most useful 
to developing their own understanding, 
but they should have some examples of 
possible ways to do it. For this reason 


Send us pictures of: 

Sites and Facilities 
Conference Workshops 
Mood and Nature 
Activities and Program 
Staff and Campers 


teachers or parents interested in en¬ 
couraging Reflective Recreation should 
get involved themselves and provide a 
commentary on the problems and 
advances in their own learning. 

Casual Practice and Exercise 
Trials Walking does not have to be 
done in a formal course, or even on 
marked out sections. It can be simply a 
form of challenge walking where difficult 
routes are taken instead of the easiest. 
Jogging and strolling can become more 
interesting and varied if they are 
punctuated with occasional deviations to 
go over or through an obstacle using the 
feet-only rule. 

Try it, have fun, and think about it!

2415 Kelwood Drive S.W. 
Calgary, Alberta T3E 3Z8

— A COUNSELLOR’S CHECKLIST by Sylvia Haynes 


-SUMMER 1986! 

When asked to do an article on leadership I thought, 
“Everything has really been said and everything that has 
been said has been said so well, it’s hard to know what to 
say”. 

But — here are some thoughts to ask of yourself and to think 
about as you begin to prepare for the important summer ahead. 
Take a moment to consider each item in turn. 

How did I get into this “leadership thing?” What do I have to 
give? Do I realize that each one of us has something to share 
... Can I look into my real self and find something very special 

— that ONLY I can give? 

Have I, as a leader, read the policy and contract, whether I’m 
hired or I’m working as a volunteer? Can I buy into that 
contract? 

How do I handle confrontations? Do I, as a leader, think 
before I act. Do I wonder why the camper is behaving that 
way? Does she come from a family conflict, is there a court 
case pending — back at home? Perhaps the camper has a low 
self esteem, perhaps he just can’t cope anymore. Can I stop 
before I act... and then do whatever is necessary in a caring, 
loving and thoughtful way. 

Can I really work with any age group or am I just saying that 
because I want to be a leader. Few of us can cope with just any 
age group for a long period of time. We all have a special age 
group with which we feel comfortable — do I know what mine 
is? 

Have I as a leader, taken advantage of the many opportunities 
there are to learn more ... from Parks and Recreation, special 
leadership courses, groups who put on seminars. For instance 

— would I as a leader know how to cope with a death — either 
at the camp — or in the life of one of my campers, (i.e. his 
relative or a friend?) Do I really know enough about the out¬ 
doors? games? skills? first aid? supervision? evaluation? 
communication? 

As a leader what kind of model am I? How can I demand that 
“my campers” be responsible, concerned, caring and loving 
if I am not that model? 

Do I as a leader remember the importance of others? How 
unique we all are! 

As a leader can I use the opportunity to learn from my 
campers? Can I share their wonder, life and God’s gifts? 

Can I stand to make mistakes and find out I’m not perfect. .. 
am I afraid this will shatter my image as a leader? 

As a leader — can I work in harmony with others — and if I 
can’t, do I have the self confidence — that I can either talk 
with the person, or confide in my section head or director — 
about the problem? 

As a leader do I take time to listen to others? As a leader can I 
take criticism? Can I act fairly? 

Do I as a leader know and accept how to be loved and how to 
love — (I’m very concerned these days about our anxiety 
about child abuse, that we as leaders don’t risk the hugs and 
touches). Am I willing to risk? Am I willing to share my 
feelings? 

As a leader have I helped my camper “into” camp as well as 
preparing them for going “out” of camp? 

As a leader how do I cope with emergencies? Have I read all 
the rules and procedures? Do I know how to do them? 

As a leader have I prepared activities, such as games, singsongs, 
for the age group I will be with? Have I tried them out? Will 
these “work” with campers who are slower, who have a dis¬ 
ability — (we all have some!!). Do I know how to adapt to 
the situation? 

Before I respond to a situation do I carefully analyse and 
assess it? Is it necessary to make an immediate decision? 


Can I define the problem? 

Who is involved? 

Having identified the problem, what are the feelings of those 
involved? 

Are there any policies to guide the decision? 

What has worked in the past? 

What is the maturity of the group? 

Are they ready and willing to resolve the problem? 

Should I defer the decision to someone else? 

And after the decision has been made: 

Is the problem resolved? 

Was it the best decision in light of the solution? 

How could the situation have been prevented? 

As a leader am I flexible? Have I got myself so well organized 
that I won’t be upset by change, or new ideas? 

As a leader do I sometimes forget “THAT GROWING UP 
CAN BE TOUGH”. 

As a leader, what is my motivation for an activity? Is it possible 
that my motivation fails to consider my campers — the real 
reason for participating in the activity? 

As a leader do I care for my campers — so that in turn they 
will wish to care for each other? 

As a leader do I take my campers suggestions seriously? 

As a leader, do I ask my campers “what do you think?” and 
then listen and act on their comments? 

As a leader, do I teach my campers “to fly” and then “set 
them free?” 

As a leader, do I follow the counsel of St. Francis? “Grant 
that I may not so much seek to be understood as to under¬ 
stand?” 

Have I read several if not all of these books? 

(1984) “Camp Counsellors Handbook”, B. Blackstock/ 

J. Latimer 

(1982) “Living, Loving and Learning”, LeoBuscaglia 
(1982) “Lead on... Counsellor”, Jack Pearse, Pat Pearse, 
John Jorgenson, Jane McCutcheon 
(1985) “Friendship”, DonPosterski 
(1984) “Learning Disabilities — Camp Director’s Guide on 
Integration”, prepared by Doreen Kronick 
(1983) “But Won’t Granny Need Her Socks?”, Knowles- 
Reeves, Kendall/Hunt Press 
(Helping Children with Death) 

(1983) “No More Secrets For Me”, Oralee Wachter 

(handling the sensitive matter of sexual abuse) 

Everything has really been said before but that doesn’t count 
for a thing unless it’s been heard, understood and become part of 
you and your summer as a leader. 

“I have to say it to myself or I lose it 
I have to remember why I’m doing things or I forget 

I have to remind me what’s important or it slips away”. 

Une Check-list du Conseiller 

Quand on m'a demande d’ecrire un article au sujet des qualit&s 
de chef, j'ai pens£, “Tout est vraiment dit et tout ce qu’on a dit a 
6t& si bien dit qu’il est difficile de savoir ce qu’il faut dire.’ 1 
Cependant-voile des questions pour se demander et pour y 
r6fl6chir comme vous commencez les preparations pour I’6t6 
important qui vient. 

II est vrai que tout est d£j& dit mais cela ne compte pas & moins

m’6chappera.” 

Cindy Herbert/Susan Russell

Canadian Camping Magazine — Prize for Writing 
Established to Honour 

MRS. ANNE NASHMAN OF CAMP WAHANOWIN 


Camp Wahanowin and the family of Mrs. Anne Nashman are 
pleased to establish an annual writing prize to honour her 85th 
birthday and 34th year in camping. The format is to be a story or 
article on a camping subject written by a staff member of a 
Canadian camp. 

The sum of the prize is $100.00. An appropriate plaque or 
trophy will accompany the cash prize. 

About Mrs. Anne Nashman 

The camp mother at Camp Wahanowin since its inception in 
1955 Anne Nashman has just celebrated her 85th birthday and is 
looking forward to her 32nd camp season on Lake Couchiching. 

Best known by campers and staff as Bubby Nash, she was born 
in Glace Bay, Nova Scotia in 1901, the daughter of an immigrant 
family who had just arrived in Canada from Romania. Her father 
worked in the coal mines of Glace Bay for two years before the 
family moved to Hamilton, Ontario where Anne grew up, moving 
to Toronto after her marriage in 1919. 

Anne Nashman has always been known as an outstanding cook 
whose skills were recognized publicly at the Summer Hotel she 
opened in Crystal Beach, Ontario in the 1940’s. She also ran a 


catering service in Toronto for several years. This background of 
tourist operator and caterer combined with her son Harold’s 
camp experience to form the team that developed Camp 
Wahanowin. The camp has enjoyed an excellent reputation and a 
loyal clientele over the years, but the most cherished memory of 
campers, staff and parents is the outstanding camp cuisine 
created by Wahanowin’s own Bubby Nash. To this day parents 
call the Wahanowin office for recipes of items their children insist 
taste better at camp! 

Anne’s expertise has been passed to Wahanowin’s chef of 23 
years who developed many of his culinary skills under Bubby 
Nash’s direction. She still combs and braids hair for campers who 
line up on Visitors Day morning at Bubby Nash’s Beauty Salon 
and continues to be a grandmother figure for campers and staff to 
see and relate to. 

In establishing this prize for outstanding writing on a camp 
theme in her name, we honour Anne Nashman’s contribution to 
Wahanowin and to the Camping Community with the hope that 
she will enjoy many more years of camping on Lake Couchiching. 

Watch for more information in the fall issue of Canadian 
Camping Magazine .

TRIALS WALKING 


Trials Walking is a challenge activity 
that can be made as easy or as difficult as 
one wishes. It can be used as a form of 
casual personal exercise or as a formal 
competition. Very little equipment is 
needed, it can be done almost anywhere, 
both mind and body exercised, and most 
of all it’s fun! 

History 

Trials Walking was developed by the 
Action Studies Team of the Calgary 
Board of Education. The Action Studies 
Team is concerned with personal com¬ 
petence, or how people learn to control 
and take responsibility for their own 
actions. The work of this group involves a 
close examination of personal powers and 
how they are explored, developed, and 
maintained. A wide variety of activities 
and experiences is essential to gain a 
useful understanding of one’s own 
powers, and the Action Studies Group 
analyses existing activities and develops 
new ones for their learning potential. 

One of the many activities examined 
was motorcycle competition known as 
Observed Trials. Observed Trials was 
invented by the Scots, the same folk who 
thought up golf, and there are some 
general similarities between the activities. 
Both involve a series of transport 
problems that are to be solved with the 
greatest economy of movements. There is 
one basic rule in each case; in golf the ball 
is to be moved along only by hitting it 
with a club; in Observed Trials the rider is 
allowed to move along only by riding a 
motorcycle. It would be much easier to 
carry the golf ball and drop it in each 
hole, or climb, slog, or crawl through an 
Observed Trials course without having to 
bring along a motorcycle. But then there 
would be little challenge, and people 
exercise and develop their powers only to 
the extent that there is some difficulty to 
be overcome. So, we go through life 
making things difficult for ourselves and 
then try to make it look as easy as 
possible. 

Observed Trials involves riding through 
a series of “sections” or short lengths of 
very difficult terrain with a minimum of 
touching the ground with one’s feet, 
without falling over, and without going 
out of bounds. The obstacles, within 
sections may be small cliffs, deep 
mudholes, loose slopes, big logs, or any¬ 
thing but simply riding through the 
section. “Dabbing” at the ground with a 
foot for support is assessed one point, but 
it might be better to put a foot down and 
take one point than risk falling down or 
going out of bounds and taking five 
points. The object is to “clean” the 
section or ride through it cleanly without 
penalty points. A Trials course may be 


made up of 15-30 sections spread out 
over many miles. Each section has its own 
marshal who observes each rider and 
records the points — hence the name 
Observed Trials. Riders have a set time 
period to complete the course, 4-8 
hours, depending on its length but it is not 
a race and individual riders can budget 
their time between studying the sections, 
riding, and getting from section to 
section. 

Observed Trials has been described as a 
combination of motorcycle riding, figure 
skating, and gynmastics. It requires 
a tremendous amount of practice to be 
good at it. However, an investigation of 
things one might learn from Observed 
Trials showed it to be one of the most 
promising and powerful activities yet 
encountered. It seemed perfect as one of 
the “Reflective Recreation” activities 
being promoted by Action Studies. There 
was one major hitch though — the 
motorcycle. 

Motorcycles are expensive, they take a 
great deal of time to learn to do well and 
there are not many easily accessible places 
suitable for Trials Riding. So, it was 
reasoned, let’s do it without the 
motorcycle. This is not an unusual trans¬ 
formation. Rallying in sports cars or 
enduro riding with motorcycles involves 
navigating from point to point within 
given time restrictions. Orienteering is 
basically a foot version of the same thing. 
Why not have a foot version of Observed 
Trials — Trials Walking! 

Trials Walking 

Trials Walking involves moving over 
obstacles or difficult ground without 
taking weight on any part of the body but 
the feet. Penalty points are assessed for 
using hands, resting or falling on a knee, 
elbow, or any other part of the body but 
the feet, or for going out of bounds. 

Trials Walking sections can be set up 
over any ground that would be difficult to 
walk on without losing one’s balance, or 
any terrain that might cause one to want 
to hold on, slide along, crawl, or roll to 
get over. Section boundaries are marked 
like downhill ski slalom courses or 
shipping channels with marker buoys. A 
colour code is used, in this case red on the 
right, blue on the left. Setting up a good 
Trials Walking section requires imagi¬ 
nation. A healthy sense of humour is also 
helpful. 

Marking a section is done with pins, 
poles, or ribbons — depending on what 
sort of boundary is needed. The purpose 
of marking is to direct movement within 
certain boundaries so that people must 
negotiate the obstacle and not just go 
around it. Since the only requirement is to 


pass with the red markers on one’s right 
and the blue on one’s left, the route in 
between can be quite varied. 

Having many possible routes is part of 
the challenge. Sometimes however, the 
open spaces between markers make for 
alternate routes that are too obvious and 
easy, so sometimes line markers are used. 

Sometimes there is a need to restrict or 
carefully judge body position in relation 
to a marker, and ground markers won’t 
do. In this case marker poles are used. 

Trials Walking courses can be set up 
over either natural or manufactured 
obstacles. Courses can be set up inside 
using saw-horses, furniture, garbage 
cans, or gymnasium equipment—any¬ 
thing that will be a challenge to walk over, 
under, or through. 

Courses may include as many sections 
as seem appropriate, and each section can 
be as close or as far from the others as 
time and stamina permit. Sections should 
be long enough to contain several 
different problems, but not so long that 
they are difficult to study or observe. 

People age four and up get the idea 
quickly and courses can be designed with 
different physical capabilities in mind. A 
good course will involve a wide variety of 
movement and planning problems. 
Anyone, including fairly young children 
can design challenging sections after they 
have walked a few—and one’s under¬ 
standing of the activity and its possibilities 
is greatly increased through designing 
sections. 

Equipment 

Red and blue survey flagging or ribbon 
is cheap, readily available, and is a 
durable and effective marking material. 
Long spikes wrapped with a short length 
of ribbon, giving two loose ends, make 
effective ground level markers. Spikes can 
also be used to pin ribbons in place as a 
line marker. Care should be taken to drive 
spikes in far enough or position them so 
that they are not a hazard should someone 
take an uncontrolled fall. 

Masking tape can be used to hold down 
ribbon when courses are set up inside, or 
over obstacles like old car bodies. 

Marker poles can be made out of 
anything safe — which means soft and 
flexible. Willow wands or other flexible 
sticks can be used, but should be 
selectively and carefully taken so as not to 
have too much impact on the environ¬ 
ment. If poles are used frequently, it is 
perhaps best to invest in a set of 
polyethylene downhill ski slalom poles, 
which are already colour coded in red and 
blue. Polyethylene slalom poles come in 
eight foot lengths and can be cut in half 


26 








for most Trials Walking purposes (an 
occasional eight footer will be required in 
advanced courses). Polyethylene poles 
can be set in soft ground or snow using a 
steel bar to punch holes. In rock, ice, or 
hard ground, metal pegs with sockets will 
be necessary. These can be made up in a 
friendly local metal shop out of scrap 
metal strap and tubing. 

For your planning, sections of average 
length seem to require a total of 30 - 40 
markers. More or less may be used 
depending on the situation. Very 
challenging sections can be marked out 
using one or two short lines and only a 
few poles or pins. 

In addition to the boundary markers, it 
is useful to have a START and FINISH 
sign for the beginning and ending of each 
section. The start sign also would carry 
the section number. Markers for start and 
finish are usually arranged so that they 
form clearcut gates. 

Other equipment will depend on needs. 
Score cards and punches will be required 
for formal competition. If there are many 
sections, and they are widely separated, 
maps will be needed. 

In designing sections and laying out 
courses, care should be taken to keep risks 
of uncontrolled falls to an appropriate 
level for the age and skill of the partici¬ 
pants. 

Scoring 

Scoring is essential in competition 
Trials Walking and useful in informal 
personal exercise to keep track of 
progress. Basically the scoring is designed 
to penalize but not prevent the use of 
handholds, crawling, sliding, or resting 
against an obstacle. The system of scoring 
gives a person a choice about whether to 
take a safe single point or risk taking three 
or more points by trying to “clean” the 
section with no penalty points. 



“A one point move 


Penalty Points Assessment 

1. Point is assessed for each instance of 

the following: 

— taking a handhold with one hand 

— resting or taking weight, without 
sliding, on any single body part ex¬ 
cept the feet; such as one hand, 
knee, shoulder, arm, or hip (taking 
weight or resting on one’s trunk — 
the bottom, back, chest, or 
stomach —is assessed three points). 

2. Points are assessed for each instance 

of the following: 

— taking handholds with both hands 

— resting or taking weight on two 
body points, except the feet 

3. Points are assessed for the following: 

— taking weight or resting on one’s 
bottom, back, chest or stomach 

— taking weight by sliding on any part 
of the body but the feet or trunk (in 
case of the feet there are no penalty 
points, sliding or rolling on any part 
of the trunk is five points). 

4. Points are assessed for the following: 

— sliding or rolling contact with the 
trunk (back, chest, stomach or 
bottom) 

— touching a marker (pole, line, or 
pin) with enough pressure to cause 
it to move 

— missing a marker or passing it on 
the wrong side. 

The maximum amount of penalty 
points possible for any section is 5, so for 
instance two 3 point penalties in the same 
section would only count as 5. 

Formal Trials Walking competitions 
may also have a time limit for the whole 
course (which may be 20 sections or 
more), with penalty points assessed for 
exceeding the time limit. A single 


competition may involve two or more 
circuits of the course. For more variety 
one circuit can be done by walking the 
sections in reverse order, that is, starting 
at the finish gate and walking with the 
blue markers on the right, and the red on 
the left. 

Reflective Recreation 

Reflective recreation is a thoughtful 
approach to activity that is very useful to 
anyone interested in powers of learning. 
The personal ability of individuals to 
direct and control their own learning is the 
most significant factor in determining 
character and lifestyle. Too much of 
contemporary life fragments experience 
and institutionalizes power so that 
individuals frequently have little sense of 
their own abilities and potential. 

We learn through experience, but not 
just in the immediate sense of developing 
specific skills, for with a little perspective 
we can also learn about our own processes 
of learning and how to direct and control 
them. Learning to do things is only a 
beginning, learning how to know how to 
do things is another step towards under¬ 
standing and control of one’s own 
actions. This broader understanding does 
not come with experience alone. It comes 
with reflection on experience. Experience 
is necessary — the more of it and the 
greater the variety the better, but it is our 
analysis of experience that develops 
wisdom. 

Which brings us back to Trials 
Walking. Some activities have more 
obvious general learning potential than 
others, that is, in some activities it is easier 
to see the learning and some of the 
principles that govern it. Trials Walking is 
such an activity.

Canadian Camping Magazine is the official publication of the Canadian Camping Association. 
Editorial offices of the Magazine are located at R.R. #1, Huntsville, Ontario, POA 1K0. 

Membership in the C.C.A., as a result of membership in a provincial camping association, 
includes a subscription to the Magazine. Non member subscription is $8.00/year. Single issue price 
is $2.00. Make cheques payable to the Canadian Camping Association. Send subscriptions, sub¬ 
missions, or address changes to the editorial offices. 

Canadian Camping Magazine is published four times yearly. Deadlines for submissions are 
October 1, December 1, February 15 and May 1. Material in Canadian Camping Magazine may 
not be reproduced in any form without the expressed written permission of the editor. Copyright 
1986 Canadian Camping Association.
